Tigers kick off free agency with Pagan deal
The deal: One year, $11.5 million

Grade: C

A key reason the Detroit Tigers finished 76-86 despite a plus-71 run differential was the bullpen: Despite finishing 12th in ERA, it ranked 26th in win probability added, so it performed worse in high-leverage situations. Out with Kenley Jansen, in with Emilio Pagan, who has been the Reds' closer the past two seasons.

Jansen was only 22-for-28 in saves in 2026, so maybe Pagan is only a small upgrade, but like Jansen, Pagan has been prone to the home run, serving up 17 in 111⅓ innings over the past two seasons. The Tigers are betting that getting out of Cincinnati -- where he allowed 12 of those 17 home runs -- will help. Pagan is a three-pitch reliever, with a splitter that he throws primarily to left-handers and a cutter he throws to right-handers. But his 95 mph fastball is rather pedestrian for a modern closer, and batters have hit 12 home runs off it the past two seasons.

Pagan is also turning 36 years old and his fastball velo dropped from 95.8 mph in 2025 to 94.9 in 2026, so there are a couple of red flags here. The Tigers had to add somebody to the bullpen, and doing so before the anticipated lockout is logical, but Pagan projects as a midtier closer rather than the elite guy Detroit needs. Kyle Finnegan and Will Vest both struggled in 2026, so the Tigers could still nab a reliable right-handed setup guy. -- Schoenfield

stories.headline: Champions League talking points: Was this a good result for Man United?
stories.summary: Gab Marcotti, Mark Ogden, Sam Tighe and Alex Kirkland run the rule over Man United's draw with Sporting, plus all the other moments that mattered from Matchday 5.
stories.body:
Matchday 5 of the UEFA Champions League league phase is in the books, with Real Madrid -- thanks in large part to some world-class play from Jude Bellingham -- topping the 36-team table with three games left to play.

Barcelona and Lille notched some impressive wins, while it was a particularly forgettable round for the five Premier League teams in action; only Liverpool were able to secure all three points on offer, romping to an easy 3-0 victory over Club Brugge.

The telenovela that is Manchester United took another turn, and Arsenal and Manchester City prepared for what could be a pivotal clash on Sunday with some stale performances.

So, what to make of it all? ESPN FC writers Gab Marcotti, Alex Kirkland, Mark Ogden and Sam Tighe are here to break down the action.

- As it happened: Another night of mayhem for Pochettino's Man United

- Lindop: Liverpool are all smiles as Wirtz, Isak start to click

- Olley: Dortmund draw shows that the jury is still out on Gyökeres

Q1. Man United continue to entertain their haters and infuriate their fans even with the new hope of Mauricio Pochettino installed as manager. Except they were thumped at Anfield on Sunday (Leny Yoro's red card didn't help) and then had to battle back to get a 2-2 draw at Sporting CP with a Youri Tielemans red card, a string of individual errors, a disallowed goal, and a dodgy referee making for another wild 90 minutes. Is it going to get worse before it gets better for Poch & Co.?
Marcotti: I think we can let Man United take a mulligan for Pochettino's first two games. He's been there less than a week, going two goals and a man down at Anfield so quickly made the game meaningless and, against Sporting, they were without Matheus Cunha and Marcus Rashford and the game was straight out of bizarroworld.

Referee Szymon Marciniak has a big reputation, but he obviously had a rough night -- though nowhere near as bad the commentators on my TV made it seem. I thought Amad Diallo's goal should have stood, but I thought Kaique was fouled for the other disallowed goal. Tielemans shouldn't be tackling like that when on a yellow, that should be obvious. And, of course, Bruno Fernandes' goal was a total fluke.

Tighe: If I were Pochettino, I'd be as perplexed as I am fuming over how the first week on the job has gone. Liverpool away was over before it began due to a refereeing mistake, then a bunch more refereeing mistakes threatened to pull the rug on Wednesday's game too.

Tielemans' red card was their fifth of the season so far, and it's only November! We panned Chelsea last year for their ludicrous lack of discipline and we should do the same for United (even if Yoro's was incorrectly given, the count is still four!).

This is a team that too easily implodes or shoots itself in the foot. Every game they play, they do something that makes the next one harder. It's really hard to win top-level football games when you do that, and who's next up? Brentford ... Pochettino's pain may endure for a little longer at least.

Kirkland: "Worse" is a high bar, given how low Man United sunk at Anfield. As Sam says, Brentford on Saturday is a tricky game. You wouldn't be at all surprised if United failed to get a win there. I'm a Pochettino sceptic -- I think he's long past his best -- and beyond the coach, United just lack quality all over the pitch. These players are not good enough. I think it's going to be a long, painful season for Manchester United, and yes, very entertaining for the neutrals.

Ogden: I'm not sure whether, when the dust settles, a battling 2-2 draw away to Sporting might be regarded as a positive outcome for United and Pochettino. It was a game of ridiculous errors by players and officials alike, but United fought back from going a goal down and had two goals ruled out which, on another day with another set of officials, may have stood. Maybe United showed some character and togetherness that Pochettino can build on, but we said that after Michael Carrick's team did the same against AS Roma and they were 2-0 down after five minutes in their next game against Aston Villa.

Gab is right to talk about the positives of injured/suspended players becoming available, but can you ever rely on Rashford and Luke Shaw to dig you out of a hole? Ultimately, I think the draw isn't a bad result and a win against RB Leipzig next month should see United qualified for the next stage, so perhaps -- perhaps -- Wednesday was a night of green shoots of recovery emerging.

Q2. Real Madrid swept to a 5-1 win at home to PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday night, conceding first (an Ivan Perisic penalty) before exploding in the second half with five goals from nine shots on target, including an absolute peach from Jude Bellingham. It's another big win for Jose Mourinho & Co. but they have looked average at times -- outplayed by Internazionale, Roma and PSV in Europe, and Celta Vigo in LaLiga last weekend -- before turning on the style. Can they win the UCL like this?
Marcotti: Of course, they can. I mean, for all the inconsistency, they've won every game they've played this season in all competitions, bar two. And as I've pointed out many times, if you have a shutdown keeper like Thibaut Courtois and a bunch of individual superstars that can score out of nothing, you can always go far in a knockout competition like the Champions League. Particularly when you have a coach like Mourinho, who has already won four major European trophies.

That said, you'd feel better about their chances if they didn't go into the hole so often and need to come from behind. In the Champions League alone it happened against PSV, against AEK Athens and against Roma. And while it looked like they had found the right set-up prior to the international break, the last two games have called that into question too.

Ogden: As Gab says, having Mourinho could be decisive this season. He is a coach with a proven track record and a group of players who just need knitting together, although doing that at Madrid can be like herding cats. But they have arguably the world's best keeper in Courtois, unquestionably the world's best midfielder in Bellingham and one of the best -- if not the best -- forwards in Kylian Mbappé. So rather than a question of "Can Madrid win it?", it should be "How can they not win it?"

With Mourinho in charge, Madrid can out-cynical Arsenal and also beat Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain in a match-up of superstars. So yes, Madrid are probably the favourites right now.

Tighe: For over a year now, I've been pretty dismissive of anyone outside of PSG winning the Champions League. It's a simple, but effective, litmus test: If you don't think a team can beat the double-reigning champs, then you can't really believe they can go all the way. But it certainly looks now as if the landscape is changing. Not only are Madrid getting better, but PSG have lost Désiré Doué and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia to ACL tears, having waved goodbye to Bradley Barcola in the summer. This makes them demonstrably weaker and opens the door for a serious challenger like Real Madrid.

Kirkland: I was at Madrid's games against Inter, Roma, RB Leipzig and PSV. And honestly, for large portions of those games, Madrid were terrible. Really terrible. Just as bad as they were last season, when they looked miles off Europe's best. Their points tally is really quite misleading: Inter and Roma were far superior for an hour, and so were PSV for 45 minutes. But yes, when they feel like it, Madrid have such an elite spine -- namely Courtois, Bellingham and Mbappé -- that when they click, they're near unstoppable. That's what happened in the last 10 minutes against Roma, and in the second half against PSV. Plus, Mourinho has tightened up the defence, and Bernardo Silva has given the midfield what it was lacking.

I still suspect that when Madrid come up against a really good team over two legs, in the knockout phase, they'll come unstuck. But with Bellingham in superhero mode, I'm not ruling out them going all the way. Remember 2021-22, when Madrid were outplayed by PSG, Chelsea, City and Liverpool, and still won it? That.

Q3. Man City and Arsenal square off this weekend in what should be the biggest Premier League game of the season, but it's not shaping up to be much of a spectacle as both teams look off the boil. City had to come from behind twice to get a home draw vs. a Napoli side that's only won three of their last 10 games in all competitions, while Arsenal lumbered to a 1-1 stalemate with Borussia Dortmund despite a nice goal from Viktor Gyökeres. Do either Arsenal or City look ready for Sunday? What's wrong?
Ogden: I think Arsenal are fine. The last two results are just part of the natural course of a season: Newcastle United is never an easy away game, and Arteta made plenty of changes against Dortmund. When Sunday comes around, they'll be at full strength (injuries aside) and you'd expect them to win comfortably because City really are in a mess right now, but where do you start?

First of all, Man City are missing Pep Guardiola's drive, tactical genius and demanding personality. The players trusted him implicitly, knew that he was a proven winner and that there was no need to question his tactics. None of that applies with Enzo Maresca, and you can see that the team is not buying into his way of playing. It's too slow and predictable, the players are losing belief and confidence and it's showing on the pitch.

Those wins at Old Trafford and Anfield earlier this season were down to big slices of luck, but luck is no longer on City's side and they're playing like a very average team.

Marcotti: Arsenal will probably be fine, as Oggy says, but mainly because City are struggling. However, I would question whether Arsenal are as good right now as they were last season (they have identical points totals after 11 games). Not sure I buy this business about how tough it is to play away to Newcastle either, when they've won just one of six at St James' Park this season. Against Newcastle they didn't have a single shot in the second half until Noni Madueke's late equalizer, and while it's true, they made a bunch of changes against Dortmund, some of the key mistakes were made by regulars like Gabriel Magalhães, who usually operates at a far higher level.

That said, City have a laundry list of issues. Many will focus on the defending and, of course, it has been subpar, as even Maresca has admitted. We know the defenders are good as individuals, so the issue is probably tactical. I'd be concerned with the attack, though. Napoli had a bunch of regulars missing, so manager Max Allegri simply played a low block and City had a lot of difficulty creating chances. They don't generate turnovers the way they did and Rayan Cherki and Phil Foden aside, there isn't much in the way of creativity either.

Maresca has to sort it out -- and I think he will -- but this squad is not particularly deep. They could use another option in central midfield because Ayyoub Bouaddi and Elliot Anderson are still very young, they could use a back-up option for Erling Haaland and another viable winger wouldn't go amiss either, especially with Antoine Semenyo out.

Tighe: Despite listing a number of issues there, I still think Mark and Gab have gone easy on City. They've been really bad recently and the post-Pep era is hitting like a hammer right now. A team with this much talent (on paper) should not be so reliant on a handful of players performing out of their minds each time. Anderson is doing the work of three midfielders, while the attack feels oddly "Cherki or bust" at times.

For Fulham to rock up at the Etihad and match them was a real eye-opener, and then an average Napoli side caused them loads of problems. This weekend's fixture may well technically see England's two best teams meet, but it won't actually feel like that when the whistle blows.

Kirkland: I disagree slightly with Mark and Gab, because I do think there are things for Arsenal to worry about.

David Raya's fitness is huge. If he doesn't make it on Sunday, Kepa Arrizabalaga is a million miles away from Raya's level. The other big issue is the left wing, where Christos Tzolis has been really disappointing and Eberechi Eze never looks comfortable. Bukayo Saka's absence on the right is also significant, even if Madueke has been surprisingly effective stepping in for the last month. In fact, the whole frontline is a problem.

Arsenal have scored just nine goals in five Champions League games and while a full 15 teams have scored more, including all of the sides above them in the league phase table. Even the midfield isn't worry-free, where Bruno Guimarães is still struggling to get up to speed in late November. Fortunately (as an Arsenal fan) City are a shambles, and even if they raise their game, Arsenal's defence is strong enough to see them through.

Q4. We worried about Bayern Munich as soon as Harry Kane went down with a serious injury, but it seems their problems run much deeper than that. The botched handling of Jamal Musiala's ongoing issues, a forward line missing Kane, Michael Olise, Serge Gnabry and Ismael Saibari, the starting of Konrad Laimer (a midfielder/fullback) up front, a blooper reel-worthy own goal from Aleksandar Pavlovic, and a 2-1 defeat at Lille, who are no world-beaters. Can Vincent Kompany figure this out before it's too late?
Tighe: This raft of injuries is definitely threatening to derail their winter. The January transfer window can't help them because it's a) one month away), and b) they get a month off soon which "covers" a decent portion of Kane and Saibari's injuries anyway. Bayern have five games left until the Bundesliga goes on pause and Kompany needs to find a solution fast.

Lennart Karl up front late on against FC Cologne didn't work. Laimer up front here didn't work either. Curiously, there's a natural striker in 19-year-old Noah Codjo-Evora in the squad, but he's played a grand total of 12 minutes off the bench so far.

Will it be Luis Díaz that Kompany turns to next? The Colombia international once moonlighted up front for Liverpool for a spell and was pretty handy...

Ogden: My natural inclination is to treat the first half of the season as prep time for the business end, March onwards, when the games really matter, but there's too much happening at Bayern to just dismiss it all as stuff that will be in the rearview mirror in the spring. In some aspects, Kane's injury is the least of their worries -- he'll be fit in three months and, although might take time to get back to full speed, will still be around when Bayern really need him.

But Musiala? That's a different story altogether and Bayern's handling of his situation betrays a sense of all not being well at the Allianz. And then there's Dortmund threatening to "do a Bayer Leverkusen" by beating Bayern to the Bundesliga title. All in all, it's hard to see Bayern being a contender for the Champions League with so many issues still to be addressed.

Marcotti: First off, can we praise Lille boss Davide Ancelotti? This was Bayern's first UCL defeat since the mad 5-4 at the Parc des Princes (I was there). Saibari can plug holes, but he's really more of an attacking midfielder and in any case he probably won't be back until after Kane. Gnabry can also do it, but he's not back until January. So based on what we know -- Kane's return is expected to be late January/early February -- it seems obvious to me that they need a body up front. You can't throw little Karl to the wolves like that, and Laimer can do many things, but play center forward isn't one of them. Díaz? Fine, but then you have a gaping hole on the wing. (Oh, and Alphonso Davies is injured too).

The best solution? Get a body in on loan, even if it means paying a healthy loan fee. Whether a veteran or a younger guy who you can try to make permanent if he works out. It's not just about the Champions League, it's about the Bundesliga too. There are nine games -- more than a quarter of the season -- between now and Feb. 6 and Bayern are second in the Bundesliga (and could be fourth come Monday). As for Musiala, read my column. This was a craven unnecessary act of self-harm.

Kirkland: I agree with Gab on Ancelotti -- I think he's potentially a really interesting coach, even if Lille's record in the Champions League this season is mixed at best. Here in Madrid, everyone was convinced that he'd go onto big things.

As for Bayern, it does feel like they've dropped off quite a bit compared to last season, and their results so far reflect that. Kane should be back by the time the knockout phase gets serious, but there are no guarantees as to when and if he can hit top form. And the Musiala situation is deeply embarrassing, for a club who -- at least from here in Spain -- you'd characterise as usually tend to do things the right way. Kompany is so impressive, but this is a big test now.

Q5. PSG look beatable, Liverpool got a big win, Bellingham scored a worldie for Real Madrid ... what else do you want to call out from Matchday 5? Your choice!
Tighe: I do think that Bellingham goal deserves a few column inches dedicated to it, and as the man who spent most of Wednesday afternoon watching it on a loop, I'll step up to the plate.

It really is a quite ridiculous goal. I suspect the list of players in today's game who are actually capable of replicating it is a short one; you might even be able to count them on one hand. It is the stuff of Ronaldinho, of Diego Maradona, of the game's great entertainers and special talents. To tee yourself up like that so cleanly that you can hit a dipping effort like that must feel so sweet, and the fact he used the outside of his boot to add some direction only upped the difficulty level.

Marcotti: I'm going to call out Roma here. They didn't just take points from PSG away, they did it their way, by playing Gian Piero Gasperini-ball all over the pitch. Sure, PSG were without Désiré Doué and Maghnes Akliouche. Gasperini decided to start with Donyell Malen, Bryan Cristante and Paulo Dybala -- all of whom are fit and three of their best players -- on the bench. And he went man-for-man all over the pitch, without any fear.

I was also struck by Mario Hermoso on the first goal. He makes a forward run, lays the ball off, and then takes a center foward's position in the middle of the box and puts it away. It's not a coincidence that Roma's defenders have scored more goals than any other group of defenders in Europe's top five leagues. Hermoso said post-game that Gasperini insists on having them make forward movements and finish in training. If you're going to go man-for-man you will be pulled into different positions and have to play, even for just a sequence or two, in roles that aren't your own. It's that sort of detail that makes Gasperini unlike most other coaches. That said, Roma are still outside of the playoff spots...

Ogden: OK, so Sam and Gab have gone for the positives -- yes, Bellingham's goal was a stunner -- but I want to single out Manchester City here. For two things. First, that horrific orange fourth kit. City have a habit of producing garish away kits -- remember the Oasis tribute outfit in 2024-25? -- but they took it a new level this time with a strip that they'll probably wear once or twice again and then ditch it for another one next year.

But the main point on Man City is the closure of the top tier of the main stand for a Champions League game. I can't think of any other major European club that would do that -- it's the Champions League, the cream of the crop. A club with such a huge commercial revenue and growing fanbase should be able to fill a stadium on a Champions League night.

Kirkland: A word about last season's semifinalists, Atlético Madrid. Their biggest problem so far this season had been in attack, and on Wednesday, two forwards who've been underperforming, Julián Álvarez and Alexander Sørloth, both found the net in their 2-0 win over Viking FK. Sørloth hadn't scored all season; Álvarez now has three goals in all competitions. Atlético might have slipped off people's radars a bit given their results so far, but don't forget they only narrowly lost to Liverpool, and beat United. Yes, Bayern outclassed them earlier this month, but if Álvarez and Sørloth can keep scoring, I think Diego Simeone's team still have a chance of making another run deep into the knockout rounds.

stories.headline: Aleksander Barkov, Brad Marchand return from injuries against Senators
stories.summary: Aleksander Barkov and Brad Marchand are in the Panthers' lineup together for the first time since the title-clinching game of the 2025 Stanley Cup Final.
stories.body:
Aleksander Barkov and Brad Marchand played a ton of hockey together in recent weeks, often with nobody watching. Such is life when players are rehabbing knee injuries alongside one another.

At long last, they're playing for real again.

The star-studded Florida Panthers got two of their biggest names back Wednesday night, with Barkov and Marchand -- who hadn't been together in a real game since the 2025 Stanley Cup final -- returning to the lineup against the Ottawa Senators.

Both had been out with knee injuries that were suffered in early October. The usually stoic Barkov was seen smiling a bit in warmups. Marchand took a long look around not long after he skated onto the ice, seeming to soak in the atmosphere.

"We know we have an incredible team this year and we can do some special things, but there's a foundation that needs to be built and you want to be part of that to go through that process," Marchand told Scripps Sports in an on-ice interview during warmups Wednesday. "It's frustrating when you're not, but it's great to be back out here with the guys."

The returns were not unexpected, though Marchand's might have come a few days before the Panthers initially anticipated. Florida made some roster adjustments this week to free up cap space needed to get both into the lineup, the clearest sign that the returns were very close.

Both appeared in only two of Florida's first 24 games this season. Barkov played the first two, Marchand played the next two, and both got hurt during their second contests of the year. But late November was always the target for both, and they evidently hit the rehab finish line together.

The lineup was largely as would be expected for their return game. Barkov was centering Florida's first line, with Carter Verhaeghe on his left wing and Sam Reinhart on his right. Marchand was on Florida's third line, with Eetu Luostarinen on the right and Sam Bennett in the middle.

In true showman fashion, Marchand got an assist on Luostarinen's goal that opened the scoring Wednesday.

"It's just the excitement of the unknown. We have no idea what we look like with both these guys in our lineup," Panthers coach Paul Maurice said earlier Wednesday, when the team revealed that Barkov and Marchand got their final clearances to return. "The core guys haven't played together since June of '25. So, there is that excitement. In some ways feels like the season starts today."

Barkov missed all of last season because of ligament tears in his right knee. He played in Florida's first two games this season, both on the road, before hurting his left knee on Oct. 1. Marchand made his season debut on Oct. 4, then hurt his knee in a game two days later.

"You can survive short-term injuries and you can keep your culture, you can keep your identity," Maurice said. "You cannot take your best player out for 100 games and keep a lot of that. So, we have to rebuild our identity now."

Both have been practicing for much of November, and much of their rehab work was done alongside one another.

"It was unbelievable to be with him during that time off. ... He looks unbelievable," Marchand said. "He's a special player."

Marchand, 38, is in his third season with the Panthers after playing his first 16 seasons with the Boston Bruins -- one of the team's top rivals. He was traded to Florida in March 2025 and helped the Panthers win their second straight Stanley Cup that season.

"Brad's been in and out of the lineup and he's just been so good for us when he's in," Maurice said. "Even last year, fairly close to a point a game and he was hurt most of that time. He's prolific."

Barkov, 31, is Florida's career leader in goals, assists and points. He was the team's leader in games as well, but since getting hurt he has ceded that spot to Panthers defenseman Aaron Ekblad.

"It's huge," Florida defenseman Niko Mikkola said about Barkov coming back. "He's the face of the team, the leader and probably our most important player."

stories.headline: Source: MLS owners agree new 16-team playoff format starting in 2027-28
stories.summary: MLS team owners have agreed on a new playoff format for the 2027-28 season featuring 16 teams, a source confirmed to ESPN.
stories.body:
Major League Soccer's team owners have agreed on a new playoff format for the 2027-28 season, one that will feature 16 teams with two rounds of home-and-home series and single elimination thereafter, a source with knowledge of the league's plans confirmed to ESPN.

The format was approved by team owners at the MLS Board of Governors meeting in Miami on Nov. 12. Aggregate goals will be used to determine the winners in the first two rounds with extra time and penalties used to break ties, though that approach could change, the source said.

The new approach to the postseason will be implemented in conjunction with the league's shift to a summer-to-spring calendar that more closely aligns with leagues in Europe.

The calendar transition will feature what is being called a "sprint season" to take place in the first half of 2027. That competition will feature a 14-game regular season, with the top eight teams from each conference qualifying for the playoffs. Each playoff round in that competition will be single elimination, culminating in MLS Cup on Memorial Day weekend.

The Athletic was the first to report the new playoff format. An official announcement is expected on Dec. 3. The source added that the new format was discussed with broadcast partners and sponsors.

The agreed-upon format for the 2027-28 season reflects a more simplified approach than what was previously being considered.

That previous format would have featured 20 teams in a double elimination system inspired by Australian Rules Football. The number of qualifiers received pushback from fans and media, with the league ultimately agreeing to scale back the number of teams reaching the postseason.

MLS has frequently modified its playoff format over the course of its existence, oscillating between best-of-three and home-and-home series, as well as whether away goals counted as a tiebreaker.

Currently the league uses a system in which 18 teams reach the postseason. A preliminary wild card round involving four teams feeds into a 16-team setup featuring a best-of-three series in the conference quarterfinal round. The conference semifinal, conference final and MLS Cup final are all single elimination.

Part of what drove consideration for the Aussie Rules format was increasing the inventory of playoff games, which typically draw the best ratings. The new format will still contain a total of 27 playoff games. The current approach features between 25 and 33 games. Reducing the number of playoff teams from 18 to 16 will also place more emphasis on the regular season.

The source also confirmed that the 2027-28 regular season will feature a revised format. Teams will be split among five divisions, and will play each of their division rivals twice, and the remainder of the teams in the league once for a total of 34 games.

While the final details still need to be approved, the league is looking at playoff qualification being determined partly by how a team finishes in its division, as well as a league-wide table. Five of the games against division rivals will take place at the end of the season to add some drama to the fight for playoffs places.

stories.headline: Williams, Alpine fined £627k by FIA for breaching F1's cost cap
stories.summary: The FIA has announced that Williams overspent by £627,000 under F1's cost cap last year, while Williams and Alpine both committed "procedural" breaches.
stories.body:
The FIA has announced that Williams overspent by £627,000 ($821, 869) under Formula 1's cost cap last year, while Williams and Alpine both committed "procedural" breaches under the sport's financial regulations for 2025.

The two teams have accepted the findings of the FIA's Cost Cap Administration (CCA) and entered into accepted breach agreements (ABAs), by which each team acknowledges their overstep and agrees to a penalty.

Williams will face a financial penalty and a 1.5% reduction in its wind tunnel and CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) time next year, while Alpine will only face a financial penalty.

Williams overspent by £627,000 last year, which equates to a 0.48% breach of the 2025 budget cap.

In a statement released by the FIA, the CCA recognised the following points.

"There is no accusation or evidence that WGPE [Williams Grand Prix Engineering] sought at any time to act in bad faith, dishonestly or in a fraudulent manner, nor that it wilfully concealed any information from the Cost Cap Administration.

"The Financial Regulations are complex, and the breaches arose from an interpretation adopted by WGPE in good faith; WGPE has accepted the FIA's interpretation and the resulting breaches.

"There is no evidence that WGPE gained or sought to gain any advantage (sporting or otherwise) from the identified breaches; and the Minor Overspend Breach amounts to £627k and therefore, with 0.48% over the 2025 Cost Cap, falls at the lower end of the

Williams also issued a statement acknowledging the breach.

"Atlassian Williams F1 Team has reached an Accepted Breach Agreement with the FIA in relation to our 2025 Cost Cap submission," the team statement said.

"The FIA has determined that the team committed a minor overspend breach and an accompanying procedural breach, unintentionally exceeding the cap by £627,000 - 0.48% over the 2025 Cost Cap. The agreed outcome is a financial penalty and a 1.5% reduction in wind tunnel and CFD testing over the next 12 months.

"The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure. We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

"The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process.

"Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future.

"We have always been and will continue to be strong supporters of the Cost Cap, which naturally requires accurate policing to be effective."

Although Alpine did not overspend in 2025, its financial reporting included inaccuracies relating to marketing activities, non-F1 activities, HR activities, employee bonus costs, offsetting of costs and costs of inventories.

As with Williams, the FIA made clear that Alpine had not acted in a fraudulent manner nor sought to gain an advantage.

Alpine accepted the findings, and its financial penalty, in a statement of its own.

"BWT Alpine Formula One Team acknowledges and accepts the findings of the Cost Cap Administration (CCA) for the 2025 Reporting Period," the statement said. "The team accepts that it unknowingly committed a Procedural Breach, which is a result of inaccuracies in the Full Year Reporting Documentation for costs related to exclusions and adjustments.

"The errors and inaccuracies in the reporting were specifically related to non-sporting and operational costs which the CCA recognised didn't give the team any performance advantage, such as Marketing Activities, non-F1 Activities, HR Activities, Employee's Bonus Costs, Offsetting of Costs, and Costs of Inventories.

"The team would also like to express its thanks to both the CCA and FIA, for its diligence and understanding throughout the entire process. The Financial Regulations are still relatively new, constantly evolving and complex, with some exclusions and adjustments being open to each team's interpretation. The team acknowledges the collective efforts it needs to make across the business and recognises where improvements can be made in future."

The other nine F1 teams were found to be in compliance with the 2025 financial regulations.

F1 introduced its cost cap in 2021 to make the series more sustainable and provide a more level the playing field between the biggest teams and the sport's backmarkers.

Red Bull was found to be in breach of the very first cost cap after it emerged it had overspent by 1.6% in 2021, resulting in a $7 million fine for the team and a 10% reduction in its wind tunnel and CFD time.

stories.headline: Sparks forward Cameron Brink, Ben Felter wed at Stanford
stories.summary: The couple met in 2021 and was engaged in 2024 before marrying at their alma mater's Memorial Church.
stories.body:
Cameron Brink and Ben Felter have officially tied the knot after holding a ceremony on Nov. 14 at their alma mater Stanford's Memorial Church.

According to a report Tuesday from Vogue Magazine, which shared behind-the-scenes details and images, the Los Angeles Sparks forward had four bridal looks, including a custom dress from bridal designer Danielle Frankel for the ceremony, and another for the reception.

Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry and his wife, Ayesha, were among those in attendance. Curry and Brink are godsiblings as their fathers were teammates at Virginia Tech, and their mothers were roommates on campus.

The reception was at Ritz-Carlton, Half Moon Bay, while vows were exchanged at Memorial Church, one of the earliest interdenominational churches in the West. The waiting list to get married there can be up to four years, but alumni receive a shorter period, according to Vogue. The couple told the magazine that they always knew they wanted to wed there.

"Walking past the ornate mosaics on my way to class was always the best part of my day," Brink said.

Brink and Felter met at Stanford in the fall of 2020. The two began dating in March 2021 after Felter sent Brink an email in which he included his phone number. Felter, who rowed at Stanford, proposed to Brink in Paris in September 2024.

The No. 2 pick in the 2024 WNBA draft, Brink averaged a career-high 9.5 points plus five rebounds and 1.8 blocks for Los Angeles in the 2026 season.

stories.headline: Price tag for Tassie's new AFL stadium goes up, again
stories.summary: The estimated cost of a new 23,000-seat waterfront venue, set to eventually become the home of the Tasmania Devils, has risen again.
stories.body:
Tasmania's new AFL stadium has suffered another cost blowout, causing the premier to break a promise to cap the state's spend as critics fear the end price will be far higher.

The cost estimate for the 23,000-seat roofed venue at Macquarie Point in Hobart has increased from $1.13 billion to $1.23 billion.

On top of the figure is $132 million for broader precinct infrastructure, project delivery costs of $183 million and unspecified contingencies, taking the total to $1.54 billion.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff previously pledged to cap Tasmania's contribution to the build at $875 million as part of a deal to get the project through parliament.

But he conceded on Tuesday the state would have to cover the slated $100 million increase via extra borrowings.

"The previous cost estimate, which we announced ... some 14 months ago, there's been a lot of water under the bridge since that point," Mr Rockliff said.

The premier confirmed the project wouldn't head back to parliament for the approval of the necessary extra funding, despite previous assurances it would.

The latest estimate reflects increases in the cost of construction, sustained high oil and materials prices, higher labour costs and its complexity, the state government said.

The stadium is expected to be ready for the 2031 AFL season and was a condition of the Tasmania Devils being granted a licence to enter into the national competition in 2028.

It initially had a price tag of $715 million.

Mr Rockliff said the state had reached out to the federal government and AFL for extra money on top of their $240 million and $15 million contributions.

Anti-stadium group Our Place Hobart said the new cost estimate failed to take into account other factors, including the interest bill and the exact cost of contingencies.

Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff described the ongoing cost increases as a deep betrayal of Tasmanians.

"Who knows where the final price for the stadium will end up?" she said.

"What we do know is there's been now a fifth major cost blowout and there's not yet a contract price locked in for this massive project."

Federal independent MP Andrew Wilkie fears the stadium will end up costing $2 billion.

"Once you add the cost of the debt over a decade, the total cost to the Tasmanian taxpayer is closer to $3.5 billion," he said.

Devils chief executive Brendon Gale said the question of any additional funding from the AFL was a matter for the sport's governing body.

"The politicians can politic. We'll get on with building our club," he said.

"People have their views and are entitled to them. But based on my experience, people never look back. These types of projects transform cities and states."

The release of updated costs came ahead of schedule after the government bowed to political pressure to make the figures public before the end of the parliamentary year.

In mid-October, BESIX Watpac was announced as the preferred builder. A final contract is set to be signed by the end of 2026.

BESIX Watpac recently built a 30,000-seat roofed stadium in Christchurch in New Zealand which cost about $540 million.

Mr Rockliff said the final contract price for the Hobart stadium was unlikely to differ from the $1.23 billion estimate.

The stadium has been deeply divisive in Tasmania amid rising state debt, a stretched health system and other under-pressure services.

The AFL and federal government have been contacted for comment.

stories.headline: 'Can't judge them': who Papenhuyzen wants at the Storm
stories.summary: Ex-Melbourne star Ryan Papenhuyzen has made some big calls on who should be the next Storm coach and the one to keep from Cameron Munster and Harry Grant.
stories.body:
Ryan Papenhuyzen empathises with Cameron Munster but believes Melbourne must prioritise keeping Harry Grant if the NRL powerhouse can't hold on to both superstars.

Munster on Tuesday rejected an offer from the Storm believed to be for one year with the option of another season, labelling the terms "disappointing".

The Storm are also fighting to keep Grant, and Papenhuyzen was unequivocal when asked on Wednesday who the club should target if salary-cap pressures meant only one of the newly crowned Australian World Cup winners could stay.

"I went through something similar as Munster where I thought the club had low-balled me," the happily retired 2020 premiership-winning hero told AAP.

"But having my time out of the game now, they've got their reasons for offering those certain amounts and it might not be enough (for Munster).

"Penrith have done it for years and years. They get to a point where they can't hold their players and they've got a price for their players.

"So I understand Munster's perspective. He wants to earn as much as he can in his career and he wants to win a premiership, so that probably limits his opportunities.

"If a club's got money and they're in a premiership window, it's probably a good chance he'll go to that club."

At 28, skipper Grant is four years younger than Munster and more important long-term to the Storm, Papenhuyzen believes.

"Harry's done a brilliant job in terms of leadership," the ex-Clive Churchill Medallist turned caddy said after playing in the Australian PGA Championship pro-am in Sydney.

"The amount of care he has for everyone in that group and the way he thinks about the game, I feel really sorry for him over the last 12 months (when Melbourne missed the finals) because he's always trying to find new ideas to bring everyone.

"He's a great leader for that club going forward. I'd hate to see him go because he's a player you want to build a club around and I guess Munster is towards the back end of his career.

"He had a great World Cup, but World Cups are different to NRL seasons. You've got to lock in for a month with that, and an NRL season's a long time."

Pressed on who he'd keep as a priority, Papenhuyzen said: "Harry's probably the one leadership-wise. Just his qualities are really admirable.

"You know what Munster brings to the game. He gives you confidence standing next to him, knowing what he's going do, but I just think Harry ..."

With coach Craig Bellamy confirming he is moving on at the end of 2027, Papenhuyzen also suspects Grant might be a better for the Storm's new mentor, whomever that may be.

"Harry's really respected and in terms of trying to keep the culture, he's very open-minded too," the BMW golf correspondent said.

"He's open to new ideas, whereas Munster is very much like Bellamy - he's sort of got his way and it's worked for him for so long.

"Whatever they both decide to do, you can't judge them. It's never a right or wrong decision."

Papenhuyzen believes it would be "awesome" if Billy Slater succeeded Bellamy, but suspects "life is too good" for the Storm legend to be a head NRL coach.

"I love Jyles. If he went back there, I'd be awfully encouraged of how well they're going to go. They'd probably be my two."

But Papenhuyzen, also open to helping out the new coach, nominated Bellamy's son Aaron as a left-field option.

"Aaron's awesome with people," he said.

"He's awesome with the wider playing group and he understands that Craig sometimes pushes the boundaries. Aaron's a bit more like Wendy - Craig's, Craig's wife.

"They're both a bit more more gentle, so you've got that loving, nurturing side and potentially (he could do the job).

"I do know you just need people around you. We'd be silly to say the coach controls everything."

stories.headline: Commanders try to continue momentum while Cardinals work to end 11-game home losing streak
stories.summary: — Some people around the NFL might have needed a reminder what Jayden Daniels can do on a football field before the quarterback led the Washington Commanders
stories.body:
GLENDALE, Ariz. -- — Some people around the NFL might have needed a reminder what Jayden Daniels can do on a football field before the quarterback led the Washington Commanders on an impressive game-winning drive Monday night.


Arizona Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur was not among them.


“He's a stud — he's a good football player,” LaFleur said. “I don't think people have forgotten that. I think he's shown that this year, particularly over the last few weeks.”


Now the Cardinals (3-8) and their revamped defense will try to stop Daniels and the Commanders (4-5-1) in the desert on Sunday. Arizona has lost three straight games and is trying to snap an 11-game home losing streak, which is the longest in franchise history and one of the longest in NFL history.


The Cardinals shook up their coaching staff on Monday, firing defensive coordinator Nick Rallis and promoting veteran coach Teryl Austin to take over for the remainder of the season. The 61-year-old Austin has plenty of experience as a defensive coordinator, spending time in the role with the Pittsburgh Steelers (2022-2025), Cincinnati Bengals (2018) and Detroit Lions (2014-17).


LaFleur said he didn't expect Austin to bring drastic changes, though he was sure there would be some tweaks.


“We've got six weeks (left) — you can't just wholesale change,” LaFleur said. “But he'll put his spin on it.”


The Commanders have moved back into the playoff race after winning three of their past four games. They'll have a quick turnaround after Monday's win, facing the Cardinals on six days of preparation.


The 25-year-old Daniels — a 2024 Pro Bowl selection — has played well over the past five games, throwing for at least 200 yards in all of them and tossing seven touchdowns and just two interceptions. He's familiar to fans in Arizona, spending the first few years of his college career at Arizona State before transferring to LSU and winning the Heisman Trophy.


Now he's playing some of the best football of his professional career.


“I couldn’t have been more proud at the end to see Jayden,” Commanders coach Dan Quinn said after Monday's win. “I thought he absolutely ripped a couple of throws in the way that he can."


Need to know
Washington (4-5-1) at Arizona (3-8)


When/where to watch: Sunday, 4:25 p.m. EST, FOX


Latest odds: Commanders by 7 1/2.


Against the spread: Commanders 6-4, Cardinals 4-7


Last week: Commanders beat the Bengals 22-20; Cardinals lost to Chiefs 34-7


Last meeting: Commanders beat the Cardinals 42-14 on Sept. 29, 2024, in Glendale, Arizona.


Series record: Commanders lead 79-47-2.


Matchup to watch
Daniels vs. the Cardinals' new-look defense. On paper, this should be another juicy opportunity for Daniels to continue his good play. Arizona has given up at least 30 points in eight of 11 games this season and has allowed a league-high 25 touchdowns in the passing game. The Cardinals also have just 22 sacks this season, which ranks in the bottom half of the league.


Stats and stuff
— Cardinals TE Trey McBride has caught a team-high 87 passes this season which ranks second in the NFL behind Dallas receiver CeeDee Lamb, who has 88 receptions.


— The Cardinals might be starting 40-year-old Josh Johnson at quarterback for a second straight week. Rookie quarterback Carson Beck is still dealing with back spasms and his availability is questionable. Johnson completed 18 of 31 passes for 155 yards and a touchdown in last week's 34-7 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs.


— Cardinals safety Budda Baker will become just the 18th player in franchise history to appear in 150 games with the franchise on Sunday.


— Arizona has lost just one fumble this season, which is the best mark in the league.


— The Commanders have a 10-3 record against the Cardinals since divisional realignment in 2002.


— Washington rookie WR Antonio Williams had a breakout game in Monday's win, catching nine passes for 122 yards, including two receptions on the game-winning drive that took just 39 seconds.


— The Commanders have won two straight games for the first time since 2024, when they won six straight games to end the regular season.


— Washington is in third place in the NFC East, two games behind the New York Giants (6-3-1) for the top spot. The Dallas Cowboys are in second with a 5-6 mark. The Commanders and Giants played to a memorable 27-27 tie in Week 5.
