stories.headline: VAR review: Why Man United should've gotten winner vs. Sporting
stories.summary: VAR often causes controversy, but how are decisions made? Our resident ref, Andy Davies, explains all.
stories.body:
The video assistant referee causes controversy every week, whether it be the Premier League, Champions League or FA Cup, but how are those decisions made and are they correct?

For the 2026-27 season, we are taking a look at the major incidents to explain the process in terms of both VAR protocol and the laws of the game. The most surprising, controversial and complicated decisions will be examined all season long right here.

Photo credit: USA Sports, NBC

Andy Davies (@andydaviesref) is a former Select Group referee, with over 12 seasons on the elite list, working across the Premier League and Championship. With extensive experience at the elite level, he has operated within the VAR space in the Premier League and offers a unique insight into the processes, rationale and protocols that are delivered on a matchday.

Sporting goal stands
Sporting CP 2-2 Manchester United (Nov. 25)
Referee: Szymon Marciniak

VAR: Piotr Lasyk

Time: 80 minutes

Incident: Sporting's Luis Suárez challenged United goalkeeper Senne Lammens as he attempted to catch a high ball. The United keeper then dropped the ball under the pressure of Suárez, with the Sporting attacker helping himself to the loose ball and scoring his second goal of the night. The on-field decision was a goal.

VAR Decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision, and the goal stood.

VAR Review: VAR were very comfortable that no offense had been committed by the Sporting attacker and cleared the on-field decision as correct.

Verdict / Insight: It was a correct call by the on-field referee to allow the goal and an equally correct non-intervention from VAR.

Lammens was clumsy with his handling, and any contact by Suárez was non-impactful on the keeper's ability to catch the ball. This unfortunately will go down as an error by the United keeper.

Man United denied winner

Time: 84 minutes

Incident: United had a goal disallowed for a foul on the Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira following a VAR review.

What Happened: Following a United corner, Sporting keeper Kaique was challenged by United's Patrick Dorgu, who appeared to jump into the Sporting goalkeeper, with Kaique pushing the ball into his own net under the pressure of the challenge.

The on-field referee initially awarded the goal. However, VAR recommended an on-field review for a possible foul on the keeper by Dorgu, and once at the screen, referee Marciniak agreed with VAR's decision and disallowed the goal.

VAR Decision: VAR didn't like the challenge by Dorgu and recommended an on-field review to the referee.

VAR Review: The VAR felt that Dorgu committed a careless upper-body foul challenge on his opponent, leading with an arm, not playing the ball and making foul contact, causing the Sporting goalkeeper to push the ball into his own net.

VAR felt that this was a clear on-field error by the referee and recommended that he watch it again at the pitchside monitor. Marciniak agreed with his VAR having viewed the replays and disallowed the goal.

Verdict / Insight: A poor VAR intervention and an incorrect decision, in my opinion -- a situation where the VAR has responded to the immediate reaction of the Sporting goalkeeper as opposed to the detail of the challenge, which is where his reasoning should sit.

As we have seen on many occasions in the UEFA Champions League, however, UEFA referees work to a different tolerance level when penalizing physical contact than the Premier League, and this incident is another example.

The foul was awarded for the leading arm of Dorgu contacting Kaique and impacting his ability to catch the ball cleanly while not playing the ball.

While the challenge by Dorgu was unwise given that he was unlikely to be able to play the ball, the facts are the goalkeeper gets his distances all wrong, loses momentary focus, and pushes the ball into his own net before any meaningful contact is made by the United player.

There are some comparing the Sporting second goal and the inconsistencies shown between the two incidents. However, the dynamics of both are completely different, with Suárez jumping almost vertically before making minimal contact, whereas Dorgu is running in and jumping towards his opponent, which was a red flag to the VAR, but the two should be judged differently.

Interestingly, however, United did benefit in a similar situation a couple of weeks ago when they scored a late equalizer against Aston Villa to snatch a 4-4 draw in the last minute of that match.

These two incidents highlight how the two competitions are refereed with different tolerance levels when considering what is recognized as foul contact, as I don't believe the goal on Wednesday would have been disallowed in a regular Premier League match.

Yoro red card vs. Liverpool in Pochettino debut

Liverpool vs. Man United (Nov. 22)
Referee: Sam Barrott

VAR: John Brooks

Time: 8 minutes

Incident: Manchester United defender Leny Yoro sent off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity (DOGSO).

What Happened: Liverpool striker Alexander Isak latched onto a forward ball and was bundled over by a clumsy challenge from Yoro. Referee Barrott was quick to send Yoro off for denying an obvious goal scoring opportunity.

VAR Decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of a red card.

VAR Review: VAR ref Brooks didn't need long to check and clear the on-field decision. It was as straight forward a check you would want as a VAR.

Verdict / Insight: A straightforward decision for referee Barrott to send Yoro off for DOGSO after eight mins as the contact between him and Isak was clear.

In DOGSO situations such as this one, the referee must quickly determine if the ball is with playing distance when the foul contact occurs from the defender, which was the case in this incident.

Such a key decision like this one, so early and obvious, would have settled any nervous energy that Barrott would have been managing in the early stages of this match. In big ticket games, any key decisions have enormous consequences. However, Yoro made this easy situation for the referee to deal with.

This was a correct decision and a positive process from the referee.

Haaland goal vs. Fulham ruled out

Man City 1-1 Fulham (Nov. 21)
Referee: Tom Bramall

VAR: James Bell

Time: 24 minutes

Incident: Man City's Erling Haaland disallowed goal for foul on Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno.

What Happened: Haaland managed to get on the end of a deep cross, directing the ball into arms of Leno. However, the Fulham goalkeeper appeared to spill the ball, and Haaland followed up his original effort and bundled the ball into the net. Referee Bramall disallowed the goal as he felt Leno had control of the ball, awarding a foul to Fulham.

VAR Decision: No goal, stuck with the referee's on-field decision.

VAR Review: A debatable outcome, where there is no conclusive evidence to prove the on-field decision incorrect, and therefore this is not an incident VAR would intervene on.

Verdict / Insight: By the laws of the game, the goalkeeper only needs to have one hand engaged with the ball for it to be deemed to be under his control.

Referee Tom Bramall had a poor view of the challenge and its circumstance. In truth, he would have used a level of experience and guesswork to reach his outcome of disallowing the goal, and it would have felt the best outcome in the moment -- I would have given the same!

However, whilst I have seen some "still" images that possibly show the goalkeeper's hands near the ball, replays show a slightly different picture where the ball looked to have been spilt by the Fulham goalkeeper and equally his immediate body language in real-time and before he had time to think for a second, told a story of a player who had made an error.

Ultimately, Fulham's Leno can think himself fortunate that this one fell his way and City can be aggrieved; it's a decision that could have fallen either way in real time.

Did Lammens interfere with Suzuki?
Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa (Nov. 8)
Referee: Chris Kavanagh

VAR: Craig Pawson

Time: 96 minutes

Incident: Possible foul in Manchester United's equalizing goal.

What happened: Bruno Fernandes swung in a last-chance corner kick as Man United threw every player they had on the pitch, including keeper Senne Lammens, into the penalty area at 4-3 down.

Patrick Dorgu outjumped the Aston Villa defenders and, with keeper Zion Suzuki flapping at the ball, nodded home what seemed like a straightforward header into the net. However, Suzuki believed he was fouled by opposite number Lammens as the United No. 1 attempted to block the Villa keeper. Lammens made contact with Suzuki while neither looking at the ball nor making any attempt to play it.

Referee Kavanagh was unmoved by the appeals, yellow-carding Suzuki for his protests and awarding the goal.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of goal.

VAR review: VAR checked the incident and was comfortable that although Lammens clearly had intent to disturb Suzuki from having a clear path to punch the ball away by bumping into him, any contact was minimal and, more importantly, his impact on the Villa keeper was a 50-50 call.

This is a ratio where VAR is not keen to get involved and will stick with the on-field decision.

Verdict: Even prominent Man United fan Mark Goldbridge was sure that VAR should have got involved. But I believe the VAR was correct not to intervene in this situation as it fell short of the threshold for a clear on-field error.

Though Lammens' intention was obvious, intent is not a punishable offense, and the many replays didn't show enough of an impactful physical action on Suzuki that met the criteria for an intervention. However, Lammens did gamble with this play, and if referee Kavanagh had judged his action differently and awarded a late free kick to Villa, United could have few complaints.

This was a borderline call either way, and I am comfortable that the on-field decision should stick regardless of which way it fell.

Arsenal robbed of a penalty
Arsenal 1-0 Hull City (Nov. 7)
Referee: Farai Hallam

VAR: Michael Oliver

Time: 42 minutes

Incident: Penalty not awarded to Arsenal for an offside offense.

What happened: Hull's Nobel Mendy appeared to grab the shirt of Kai Havertz as the Arsenal attacker attempted to get on the end of a ball into the box.

In a confusing twist and following a VAR review, Hallam explained to the stadium that a foul action had been committed by Mendy, but Havertz was in an offside position and therefore the decision was no penalty and a restart of an indirect free kick to Hull.

VAR decision: VAR recommended an on-field review for a possible penalty to Arsenal.

VAR review: Oliver asked Hallam to review the possible penalty to Arsenal at the pitchside monitor. Once at the screen, Hallam agreed that a foul had been committed by Mendy on Havertz, however he also determined that Havertz was in an offside position when the ball was played and therefore the outcome should be a defensive free kick to Hull and not a penalty to Arsenal.

Verdict: In a complex and confusing set of circumstances, the law was incorrectly applied in this incident by Hallam. A penalty should have been the outcome, and fortunately for him and ProRef, Arsenal went on to win the game, which will dampen any fallout from the situation.

What the law says: If a player in an offside position is fouled before or without committing an offside offense, the foul is to be penalized.

I have some sympathy for Hallam, as the judgment of when a player should be judged as impacting an opponent can be open to interpretation. The positioning of Havertz and the possibility of him impacting on Mendy's next action has clearly caused a misread of the situation with the referee applying the law incorrectly.

Between the referee, Oliver and his assistant VAR, the correct outcome should have been reached, and the "live comms" will be interesting when they are released. I have been a big advocate of "live comms" being available, and this is another incident when some much-needed clarity was needed in real time, which could easily have been communicated and explained.

Liverpool denied a penalty in close game?

Liverpool vs. Arsenal

Referee: Andy Madley

VAR: Stuart Attwell

Time: 34 mins

Incident: Possible penalty to Liverpool

What happened: A cross into the Arsenal penalty was nearly headed toward goal by Alexander Isak, but it appeared that he was having his shirt pulled by Jurriën Timber. Referee Andy Madley was unmoved and play continued.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of no penalty.

VAR review: An interesting incident for VAR to check. However, once reviewed they felt the contact fell short of a clear on-field error and cleared the decision.

Verdict: This incident will be a major talking point, and Liverpool can feel aggrieved that there was no intervention by VAR for this holding offense by Timber. In real time it looked like a foul act by Timber; however, it would have been difficult for Madley to be sure how impactful the contact was from his position at pitch level, and so a non-decision in the moment is understandable.

This season, VAR has been encouraged to set a high bar and not intervene unless an on-field decision is clearly incorrect. The man in the hub on this occasion, Stuart Attwell, clearly felt this fell short of this threshold. However, when analyzing the incident, the action by Timber was deliberate; he made no attempt to play the ball and acted with the sole motivation of impacting Isak's ability to head the ball toward goal, in which he succeeded.

When such a deliberate action has a direct impact on an opponent's ability to play the ball, this must be penalized. In my opinion, Attwell fell short of his responsibilities by not recommending an on-field review and this will go down as an error by VAR in a key Premier League match.

Did Lisandro Martinez deserve a red card?

Chelsea 2-0 Manchester United (Oct. 31)
Referee: Peter Bankes

VAR: James Bell

Time: 61 minutes

Incident: Chelsea were awarded a penalty following a VAR on-field review, and Lisandro Martínez was sent off for committing a second yellow card offense.

What happened: Man United defender Lisandro Martínez seemed to lead with his arm, contacting with the head of Chelsea's Wesley Fofana with an aerial challenge.

VAR decision: VAR recommended an on-field review for a possible penalty following the reckless challenge by Martínez on Fofana.

VAR review: With no decision on the field by referee Bankes, VAR felt uncomfortable with this challenge but could only intervene if he felt the referee had made a clear error.

Following several replays, the VAR felt that the challenge met the criteria for a clear foul and a missed incident by the referee, explaining that Martínez's act was clearly late, made no attempt to play the ball as he was facing his opponent and not the ball. And, most importantly, that the contact with his arm was a reckless action.

VAR recommended that the referee reviewed the challenge at the pitchside screen. Once at the monitor, the referee agreed with his VAR, awarded the penalty and issued a second yellow card to Martínez and sent him off.

Verdict: A correct intervention from VAR with a penalty and a second yellow card for Martínez the right outcome.

The challenge by Martínez was a poor one; by leading with his arm when making an aerial challenge and connecting with an opponent, there was always a very high chance that a yellow card would follow.

It was surprising that referee Bankes did not award the penalty in real-time, as the reckless contact by Martínez looked clear on first sight. On reflection, he'll be disappointed.

However, credit to the VAR. With the emphasis this season on minimal interventions and the pressure that surrounds their every action, it was a positive decision to recognize that this clear error needed correcting.

Why was Matheus Cunha's goal disallowed?

Time: 34 minutes

Incident: Man United's Matheus Cunha had a goal disallowed for offside.

What happened: A deep Man United corner was headed back across goal by Harry Maguire and nudged into the back of the net by Cunha. However, following a quick VAR check, Cunha was deemed to be in an offside position and the goal was disallowed.

VAR decision: A factual decision to disallow the goal for an offside offence.

VAR review: A quick check with the use of the semi-automated system (SAOT) clearly showed that Cunha's left leg was in an offside position when the ball was played by teammate Maguire.

Verdict: Not a clear or easy decision to make in real time, however the goal was correctly disallowed with the use of SAOT as Cunha's leg strayed beyond the last defender when Maguire played the ball back across the box.

No need for an on-field review by the referee in this situation, as this was a factual decision.

Why did Man United's Heaven avoid red card for two-footed tackle?

Manchester United 0-3 Bournemouth (Oct. 25)

Referee: Jarred Gillett

VAR: Paul Howard

Time: 37 minutes

Incident: Possible red card for Manchester United's Ayden Heaven

What happened: United defender Heaven flew into a challenge on Bournemouth's Evanilson. His tackle looked dangerous -- it was over the top of ball and both feet off the ground. Referee Gillett issued a yellow card to the defender, with disgruntled Bournemouth players expecting the card to be red.

VAR decision: VAR agreed with the on-field decision of a yellow card and cleared the decision as correct.

VAR review: The on-field communication from Gillett would have guided the VAR into a non-intervention as the description of the challenge was accurate to the replays reviewed.

Only a clear error or a complete misread of the challenge would have instigated an on-field review from the VAR. The referee described the challenge as reckless, showing a disregard for the safety of his opponent, and the VAR agreed with this reading of the incident and a yellow card outcome.

Verdict and insight: A correct outcome on-field and non-intervention by VAR; this challenge did not meet the threshold for a red card for a Serious Foul Play (SFP) tackle.

While an area of judgment, the tipping point between red and yellow card outcomes is normally based around level of contact on an opponent. The action by Heaven did tick some of the SFP boxes when considering a sanction, however the fact that there was no contact or any real danger to Evanilson, met a yellow criteria card.

It showed a disregard for an opponent's safety by his recklessness, but nothing more.

Should Brentford's Yarmoliuk have been sent off?
Brentford 1-2 Liverpool (Oct. 17)
Referee: John Brooks

VAR: Darren England

Time: 45 + 3 minutes

Incident: Brentford defender Yehor Yarmoliuk sent off for violent conduct.

What happened: With Liverpool setting up for a corner kick and time ticking away at the end of the first half, Brentford defender Yarmoliuk and Liverpool's Jérémy Jacquet clashed, with the Liverpool player ending up on the floor.

Following a lengthy VAR review, referee Brooks agreed with the VAR recommendation and finally sent Yarmoliuk off for committing a violent action and headbutting Jacquet.

VAR decision: VAR overturn. Red Card for violent conduct.

VAR review: England took time to recommend an on-field review, as Yarmoliuk's violent action wasn't conclusive from all replay angles. However, the penalty-area tight camera eventually gave him the clear evidence he needed to ask John Brooks to visit the pitch-side monitor and review the incident.

Verdict and insight: A correct VAR intervention in this incident, with Brentford's Yarmoliuk committing a violent action towards his opponent and the red card an expected outcome.

Like Rodrigo Bentancur's red card for Spurs in the last match round, when a player deliberately heads at an opponent and makes contact, it is very likely to end in a red card.

The four minutes it took VAR to reach the point of an on-field review is frustrating, as this should have been cleared up a lot quicker -- this will be something ProRef will need to improve moving forward.

Additionally, some discussion as to why the restart was not a penalty kick, considering it was a defender committing an offense on an attacker in the penalty area. However, the ball was not in play when the incident occurred and therefore the original corner restart was correct.

Was Gravenberch wrongly sent off in Liverpool-Man City?
Liverpool 0-3 Man City (Oct. 11)
Referee: Chris Kavanagh

VAR: Paul Howard

Time: 62 minutes

Incident: Liverpool's Ryan Gravenberch sent off for a second yellow card at a key stage in the match

What happened: Having already received a yellow card early in the match, Gravenberch fouled City's Jérémy Doku and received a second yellow card from Kavanagh.

VAR review: Newly introduced into the Premier League this season, second yellow cards can now be reviewed by VAR, but only if they are factually incorrect, and this situation does not fit this category.

Verdict and insight: Most won't like this second yellow card decision, and it will be viewed as "soft." However, Kavanagh was put into a difficult position by Gravenberch's late, clumsy challenge on Doku, which clearly denied the Man City attacker a promising attack as he had clear opportunity to attack Liverpool in a positive area of the pitch. The subsequent yellow card was not a surprise.

These situations are the worst type of situations for referees, because you really want a second-card offense to be undebatable and obvious to everyone. Technical offenses can be questioned and heavily debated, regardless of whether the referee is correct in law.

Gravenberch can feel aggrieved by his first yellow card. From the replays, it looks like the referee misjudged the contact made by the Liverpool midfielder on Elliot Anderson, and on reflection, a free kick alone would have been a better outcome. However, once a player is on a yellow card and challenges an opponent from behind, as Gravenberch did on Doku, the player is running a very high risk of receiving a second yellow if the challenge is a foul and has consequence.

Liverpool will feel hard done by, but the second yellow card was a correct call from the referee.

Should Man United have gotten a penalty at Fulham?
Fulham 1-1 Man United (Sept. 20)
Referee: Peter Bankes

VAR: Nick Hopton

Time: 86 minutes

Incident: Possible penalty to Man United for a handball

What happened: Man United's Lisandro Martínez felt he should have earned a penalty when he fired the ball at Fulham defender Calvin Bassey from close range and the ball struck Bassey's arm. The referee did not feel it was an offence and waved away the appeals for a penalty.

VAR decision: VAR agreed with the referee's interpretation of the incident, that the ball was struck at close range, defenders' arms were close to his body and within bodyline and therefore not a handball offence. VAR checked and cleared the on-filed decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: While Man United might have wanted the penalty, this was a correct on-field decision by the refereeing team and non-intervention by VAR.

This incident is a good example of how the handball law can create confusion in these types of situations. When the ball is struck at close range, the law is clear that the referee should allow play to continue if the player's hand or arm movement is the result of a natural reflex to potentially protect the player's face, and if such action does not make their body unnaturally bigger.

Additionally, if arms are within the body line and the ball would have struck the body/face this should also be taken into consideration when applying this law.

Bassey's reaction falls within this interpretation and was a good read by the on-field assistant referee, who would have led the communication in this incident.

Was Rice lucky not to be sent off at Brighton?
Brighton & Hove Albion 3-0 Arsenal (Sept. 19)
Referee: Darren England

VAR: Tim Wood

Time: 90 + 7 mins

Incident: Possible red card for Arsenal's Declan Rice

What happened: Rice picked up a late yellow card when he appeared to kick out at Brighton's Malick Yalcouyé in an off-the-ball incident.

VAR decision: The on-field decision of yellow card was checked and cleared as correct by the VAR.

In these types of situations, VAR involvement can be triggered only if they believe the on-field refereeing team missed a violent act or an act or brutality. VAR was comfortable that the action by Rice did not meet either threshold, so the check was a straightforward one.

Verdict: This frustrated act by Rice was picked up in real time by the fourth official and certainly high risk, when considering many off-the-ball, non-footballing offenses are often interpreted as a red card offense by referees and matched by the expectations of football, so Rice can consider himself fortunate. However, I am comfortable that this action in isolation was a frustrated and petulant attempt at a trip on Yalcouyé and not a violent act or act of brutality, therefore a yellow card feels like a correct and sensible outcome.

VAR would never get involved in this situation unless there was clear evidence that the on-field outcome was incorrect, so the yellow card was correctly checked and cleared. Rice is very fortunate that the original on-field interpretation of his action was only a yellow card, otherwise he would be serving a three-game ban following the international break.

Why was Phil Foden sent off in the Manchester derby?

Manchester United 0-1 Manchester City (Sept. 13)

Referee: Michael Oliver

VAR: Matt Donohue

Time: 23rd minute

Incident: Red card for Phil Foden of Manchester City

What happened: City's Foden appeared to kick out at United's Bruno Fernandes following an untidy tangle between the two players.

VAR decision: The VAR checked and confirmed the red card for violent conduct by Foden as a correct decision.

VAR review: The VAR had a straightforward check to confirm this on-field decision, as there was a clear kick out from Foden into Fernandes' body. The pictures aligned with the on-field comms from referee Michael Oliver, and this was a simple VAR process.

Verdict: Foden can have no complaints as he lost his composure in this situation.

There might be some debate around the level of contact of Foden's action. However, when you kick out in nature that Foden did in this moment, it is very likely that a red card for violent card will be the outcome, regardless of level of contact.

Referee Oliver was very quick with his decision, but his positioning was excellent, allowing him all the available information to reach his outcome. Additionally, it was a straightforward review for the VAR, and he correctly checked and cleared the decision having considered all the dynamics of the incident.

Why was Enzo Fernández not ruled offside in Man City's goal?
Manchester United 0-1 Manchester City (Sept. 13)
Time: 60th minute

Incident: City awarded controversial winning goal

What happened: Erling Haaland scored what looked like a goal that would be disallowed for offside. However, following a long VAR check, the goal was awarded and City took a significant lead.

VAR decision: The VAR overturned the on-field decision and awarded a goal, judging that Haaland was onside before he tapped into the United net.

VAR review: There were two key elements in this offside goal review. First, semi-automated technology showed that Haaland was in an onside position when the ball was crossed by his teammate. Second, the VAR had a subjective decision to make; did Man City's Enzo Fernández either play the ball or impact on Man United center back Lisandro Martínez's ability to play the ball given that Fernández was in an offside position and in front of the goal?

The VAR was comfortable that Fernández didn't meet any of the offside criteria and advised the referee that a goal should be the outcome.

Verdict: This was an incorrect decision by the VAR to award a goal to City, a controversial outcome that will create a lot of noise in the coming days.

What was correct: the factual aspect of the decision, which showed that Haaland was onside when the cross was played. Technology is now applied in these situations, and pictures clearly showed the position of the City attacker behind the leg of United's Dorgu.

However, the subjective element of this decision is where the VAR has made his error. There are two significant sections of law that the VAR did not apply in this moment, which should have resulted in a different outcome and the goal disallowed. It should be deemed an offside offense when (A) A player clearly attempts to play a ball that is close when this action impacts an opponent, or (B) A player makes an obvious action that clearly impacts the ability of an opponent to play the ball.

In this situation, Man United's Martinez was clearly impacted by the position and action of Fernández. Martinez's ability to defend the ball was certainly affected by Fernández, and this should have been recognized within the VAR review.

The process in this situation should have been an on-field review, when the referee comes across to the screen and views the incident himself. This would have been a subjective decision and therefore only the referee can make the final decision.

Soccer doesn't like what it doesn't understand, and this was a confusing situation for everyone. The incident will be viewed as a big error and ultimately game-changing.

Should Sunderland have been given a penalty vs. Arsenal?

Sunderland 0-2 Arsenal (Sept. 12)

Referee: John Brooks

VAR: Stuart Attwell

Time: 54 min

Incident: Penalty awarded to Sunderland

What happened: With the score 0-0 early in the second half, Arsenal were left frustrated as defender Ezri Konsa was adjudged to have fouled Sunderland's Dan Ballard after a Sunderland corner, and referee John Brooks pointed to the spot.

VAR decision: VAR checked and confirmed the on-field decision of a penalty kick to Sunderland.

VAR review: Brooks' live comms described Konsa's actions on Ballard as being "all over him at the near post, facing the wrong way." Having considered the communication from the referee, VAR ruled that he was accurate in his description and his rationale for awarding a penalty kick, and confirmed the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: With the heightened profile, focus, and referees asked to be more assertive in set-play situations such as corners, there was a high chance that a small number of penalty kicks would be awarded incorrectly, and this was an example of it playing out in real-time.

From the referee's on-field position, this incident would have looked like Konsa was clumsy with his contact on Ballard. As both players fall to the ground, referee Brooks believed that it was the Arsenal player who was pulling, deliberately facing away from the ball and committing a holding offense -- the type of foul the football world was hoping would be penalized this season.

However, from the replays, it was clear that though Arsenal's Konsa engaged with Ballard with normal contact, Ballard using his left arm to pull Konsa's shirt made the Arsenal defender spin and land on the Sunderland center back. Any punishable offense was, in fact, committed by Ballard and the restart should have been a defensive free kick.

Mikel Arteta was fuming afterwards and it's difficult to understand why VAR did not intervene in this situation given the information available to him, as it was a clear but understandable on-field error by the referee -- the referee's live description of the incident did not match the replay pictures, and this should be a red flag to the VAR.

This was a poor non-intervention by VAR, and an on-field review should have been recommended.

Why was Forest's Williams denied a winner vs. Spurs?
Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham (Sep. 5)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Peter Bankes

Time: 67 min

Incident: Possible handball to Forest

What happened: Forest defender Neco Williams thought he had given his team the lead as he bundled it across the Spurs goal line. However, VAR overturned the goal for a handball offense.

VAR decision: VAR checked the referee's call of a goal for Forest and determined that Williams handled the ball immediately before scoring and recommended that the goal be disallowed.

VAR review: This was a difficult review for the VAR, which involved multiple angles and replay speeds to determine if this goal should be allowed to stand.

VAR Bankes would have been uncomfortable with the way Williams bundled the ball into the goal, as there was very high chance that it had struck his arm. However, even if the contact was accidental, the law states that any touch of the arm by the goalscorer immediately before a goal must be disallowed.

The in-goal camera provided the decisive information, as it showed the ball striking the arm of Williams as he threw himself in to try and score, creating a change in trajectory of the ball and resulting in a goal -- VAR recommended to the referee that he should disallow the goal for a handball.

Verdict and insight: Not an easy process for the VAR to review. However, once you see the decisive replays from inside Spurs' goal, it is a straightforward decision for the VAR, as the law dictates the outcome.

With so much debate surrounding the Harry Maguire "handball goal" from last week -- when the ball struck the arm of Maguire before his shot was deflected into the goal off a defender, meaning Maguire was not the actual scorer -- this scenario is far clearer and the correct outcome is reached.

How new standards cost Arsenal a clear penalty
Aston Villa 0-1 Arsenal (Aug. 31)
Referee: Jarred Gillett

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 9 mins

Incident: Possible penalty to Arsenal

What happened: Arsenal's Bruno Guimarães was screaming for a penalty after he was challenged from behind by Villa's Ian Maatsen inside the box. Referee Jarred Gillett waved away the appeals.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of no penalty.

VAR review: VAR James Bell clearly applied the new "high bar" for intervention when he cleared this decision, taking the view that the referee's on-field decision not to award a penalty to Arsenal was not a clear and obvious error. After reviewing the replays, VAR quickly checked and cleared the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: For me, this was a clear penalty kick that should've been awarded to Arsenal. I was surprised it was not given on-field by match referee Gillett, and equally surprised the VAR did not recommend a pitch-side review.

The decision by Villa's Maatsen to challenge in the nature he did, from behind with a scissor action and no opportunity to play the ball was a poor one. By making contact only with Guimarães and none on the ball, there can be little doubt that it met the threshold for a foul -- and it took place inside the penalty box.

The surprising non-intervention by VAR is a result of the Premier League's desire this season to have less involvement and only very clear errors to be corrected, with a new "higher bar" for interventions to be applied.

It's a positive principle that should result in less time spent re-litigating decisions, yes. However, this was clearly a mistake from the on-field referee not to award a penalty and, in my opinion, this was an intervention that has been missed by the VAR team.

Arsenal winning the game will cover the narrative to some degree, however, if this was a deciding moment that cost Arsenal all three points, the profile of the incident would've been significant.

The high bar will absolutely improve the game and lower the expectations from football that VAR should get involved in everything, however it is so important that clear fouls in the penalty area, like this situation, do not get overlooked when the referee has mis-read a key moment.

Why did Maguire's obvious handball not cancel goal?
Manchester United 5-2 Ipswich Town (Aug. 30)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Jarred Gillett

Time: 56th minute

Incident: Possible handball in lead-up to Man United's second goal by Harry Maguire

What happened: The ball was cleared out of Ipswich's box toward Maguire, and the ball appeared to strike the arm of Maguire. He brought the ball to his feet and struck the ball toward goal, where it then took a grave deflection from Ipswich defender Jacob Greaves before going into the goal. Following a VAR review, the goal was allowed to stand.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of goal for Manchester United was checked and confirmed by VAR, who deemed that Maguire was not the immediate goalscorer after an accidental handball.

VAR: "It's an own goal and the accidental handball is not punishable, so we recommend you award the goal."

VAR review: With the knowledge that the ball had clearly struck the arm of Maguire, the VAR had two key elements to consider:

(1) Was Maguire's shot on target before it struck Greaves and entered the goal? In other words: was Maguire the goalscorer?

(2) Was the handball by Maguire accidental or a punishable as an intentional handball offence?

The answers to both questions could have resulted in a different outcome, but the VAR determined that it was clearly an own goal by Greaves, meaning Maguire was not the scorer, and that the handball incident was accidental. Both details meant the ball striking the arm of Maguire was negated in law, and the VAR recommended to the referee that the goal should be awarded.

Verdict and insight: It's understandable that Ipswich Town will feel hard-done by the decision.

If Maguire had scored the goal, then his handling of the ball in the lead-up would've canceled out the goal. It's only because it took the massive deflection that changed the trajectory of the ball that Maguire's incidental handball did not result in the goal being overturned.

In truth, it was a 50/50 decision that could have fallen the other way if the judgement of VAR was a different one. But the law doesn't allow a goal to be disallowed in this situation if the handball by Maguire was judged as accidental.

The subjective nature of handball in general is a confusing element of the game, and if VAR had judged this as a punishable handball and disallowed the goal, it would certainly have been a credible outcome given the context of the situation in my opinion -- and a more comfortable outcome for football.

However, the judgement by VAR Jared Gillett was not an incorrect one, with Maguire challenging for a bouncing ball and his arms in front of his body, the ball striking his left arm can certainly be deemed as accidental. It was on this occasion, with Man United the benefactor of it in this situation, and Ipswich rightfully feeling hard done by.

Should Liverpool have been bailed out by penalty?
Newcastle United 2-2 Liverpool (Aug. 23)
Referee: Stuart Attwell

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 6 mins

Incident: Penalty awarded to Liverpool for a challenge by Lewis Hall on Victor Muñoz

What happened: Liverpool's Muñoz charged into the Newcastle penalty area late into the game, and Hall made a clumsy challenge bringing the Liverpool player to the ground. Referee Stuart Attwell pointed to the spot for a late penalty for the Reds.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of penalty for the challenge by Hall on Muñoz was checked and confirmed by VAR.

The referee: "He doesn't play the ball. He makes clear contact."

VAR: "It's knee into thigh contact. Confirming the on-field decision of penalty."

Verdict: This was a correct decision made by referee Atwell and his assistant, and a decision I felt was clear in real-time.

In this type of situation, with an attacker moving into the penalty area at speed with the ball under control, any challenge by a defender must successfully play the ball or they run a very high risk of committing a foul.

Hall was naïve to make his clumsy challenge in the manner he did, and Muñoz was too clever for the Newcastle defender. This was a clear foul by Hall, and a penalty kick a correct outcome.

While it may feel to Newcastle fans that Liverpool were bailed out and gifted a draw after middling performance, Hall's foul was needless and to blame for Liverpool equalizing.

stories.headline: Fantasy baseball reactions to MLB offseason trades, signings
stories.summary: Track all the latest MLB free agency and trade news with fantasy baseball analysis from Tristan H. Cockcroft and Eric Karabell.
stories.byline: Tristan H. Cockcroft and Eric Karabell
stories.body:
Tracking the offseason MLB trades and signings with fantasy baseball implications for the upcoming season, Eric Karabell and Tristan H. Cockcroft will analyze and provide an outlook for all of the key players involved.

Players were allowed to sign with new teams beginning Nov. 2, although typically things don't really start to heat up until the league's annual winter meetings. This year's meetings are scheduled to take place in San Diego from Dec. 7-9. However, with the current collective bargaining agreement expiring Dec. 1, players and teams alike might end up waiting until after the dust settles on negotiations and a potential lockout before inking any new deals.

In any event, as any contracts are signed or trades get agreed to, this is the place to find all of the fantasy fallout of those deals. Be sure to check back throughout the hot stove season for updates.

Latest updates include the Detroit Tigers signing Kevin Gausman, the Miami Marlins signing Gary Sanchez, the Kansas City Royals signing Alec Bohm, the Toronto Blue Jays signing Japanese star Kaima Taira, the Chicago Cubs signing both Trevor Rogers and Teruaki Sato and Freddy Peralta signing with the Baltimore Orioles.

Below, you will find a list of some of the top free agents at each position. Players labeled with a (Q) received a qualifying offer from their current team and had until Nov. 17 to accept it or decline and become a free agent. Players coming from Japan/Korea who were posted by their current team have a Dec. 1 deadline to reach a deal with an MLB club to play in the United States in 2027.

Note: Not every transaction warrants the attention of fantasy managers, but for those signings and trades that do merit analysis, you'll find them listed below. Players will be separated by position and then listed in chronological order of the move within each positional grouping, with the latest news coming first. Also included are links to any standalone analysis stories and/or videos regarding major free agent signings and trades. Players who end up re-signing with their previous team will not always be included.

Jump to:

Catcher | First base | Second base | Shortstop | Third base

Outfield | DH | Starting pitcher | Relief pitcher

Catcher
Gary Sanchez signs with Marlins
Sanchez, 33, joins his seventh franchise after hitting .209 with 12 home runs as a backup for the champion Brewers. Those statistics may not seem like much, but combined with his 46 walks, and even with only 275 PA, that was enough to make him a top 25 catcher in ESPN points formats. He averaged 1.8 fantasy points per game, better than Salvador Perez, Cal Raleigh and J.T. Realmuto, among others, as only 10 catcher-eligible options drew more walks. Sanchez should work in tandem with young, lefty-hitting backstop Joe Mack, and it may mean the enticing Agustin Ramirez, a bad catcher but provider of 21 home runs and 16 stolen bases in 2025 (he spent half of 2026 in Triple-A), is not in the team's future plans. -- Karabell (11/25)

Some free agents: Carson Kelly, Kyle Higashioka, James McCann, Travis d'Arnaud, Austin Hedges

First base
Paul Goldschmidt signs with Mets

Goldschmidt, 39, hit only .252 over 380 PA with the Yankees last season -- but how he did so explains why the Mets coveted him. Goldschmidt hit .299/.393/.573 with 11 home runs versus left-handed pitching, one year after posting a .336/.411/.570 line. He has not enjoyed recent success against right-handed pitching. The Mets figure to platoon Goldschmidt, perhaps with lefty-hitting Jared Young. While that should be productive for the team, it isn't so great for fantasy managers.

Goldschmidt finished outside the top 50 first basemen in 2026 scoring. Roster him in daily formats, when you can take advantage of knowing exactly when he will be in the lineup. Fade him in standard leagues. -- Karabell (11/23)

Jake Bauers signs with Red Sox
Bauers, 31, comes off the best season of his journeyman career, posting an .873 OPS with 26 homers and 86 RBIs for the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers. He admits that he considered retirement as recently as two years ago, but he stuck around for the health benefits. Good timing. Bauers gets a four-year deal with the Red Sox, where he and right-handed-hitting Willson Contreras should make for a formidable 1-2 punch in the middle of the lineup, while sharing 1B/DH duties.

While Bauers was a top-40 hitter in points formats and roto/categories leagues last season, fantasy managers probably shouldn't expect the same kind of production moving forward, even as he performs half the time at hitter-friendly Fenway Park. Bauers had never hit more than 12 home runs in any prior season and, even now, he remains a career .223 hitter with a 2.0 career WAR.

Maybe the solid 16.3% walk rate and .218 ISO will continue, but preliminary results in NFBC drafts have Bauers going just inside the top 150. Perhaps he gets a bump for heading to Boston, but likely only a modest one. -- Karabell (11/13)

Other free agents: Josh Bell, Ryan Mountcastle, Nathaniel Lowe, Ty France

Second base

Some free agents: Gleyber Torres, Jeff McNeil, Luis Arraez, Jazz Chisholm Jr., Jonathan India, Gavin Lux, Brandon Lowe (Q)

Shortstop
Ha-Seong Kim signs with Tigers
Kim couldn't have had a much worse 2026, from his appearing in only 51 games (primarily due to issues with a finger he injured when he slipped on a sheet of ice in his native Korea in January) to his tying for the third-lowest OPS+ (2) of any player with at least as many as his 147 plate appearances during the divisional era.

The Tigers might have designs on his being their everyday shortstop, but he's more likely to be yet another infielder they can shuffle around -- good news for you Kevin McGonigle keeper/dynasty managers, as it heightens the chances McGonigle will again earn dual qualification at shortstop and third base.

Kim is only a low-end SB option for deep mixed and NL-only rotisserie leagues, barring an absolutely standout spring. -- Cockcroft (11/24)

Other free agents: J.P. Crawford, Mauricio Dubon, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Amed Rosario

Third base
Alec Bohm signs with Royals
Bohm, 30, who attended college at Wichita State in Kansas, heads closer to home after a polarizing seven-season run with the Phillies. Bohm finished runner-up for the 2020 NL Rookie of the Year award, made the 2024 All-Star team and knocked in 97 runs in consecutive seasons, before adding 88 more this past season. Miscast as a power hitter despite his 6-foot-5 frame, Bohm averaged only 14 HRs during the past five seasons in 596 PA, but he piled on RBIs because nearly half his career plate appearances came in the Nos. 4 and 5 lineup spots. Both should continue -- the RBI chances and lineup placement -- in Kansas City.

The Royals coveted a right-handed bat for the middle of their lineup. Bohm, replacing the traded Maikel Garcia at third base, should bat fourth/fifth most of the time, just like he did in Philadelphia. He should knock in runs, just like he did in Philly, because SS Bobby Witt Jr. and others will be on base. Contact-oriented corner infielders are rare in this era. Even so, only 14 third basemen scored more fantasy points in 2026. Bohm has a low strikeout rate, and he performs better versus left-handed pitching, though the change in home ballparks certainly won't help.

Defensively, um, while he made improvement at third base, it's not good news. Fantasy managers generally don't want to know unless it costs the player his starting role -- and that won't be an issue here. Let's just say Kansas City's contact pitchers (like Michael Wacha) will not be pleased by swapping out Gold Glover Garcia for Bohm at the hot corner. -- Karabell 11/25

Teruaki Sato signs with Cubs

Sato, 27 and the defending Nippon Central League Triple Crown winner, reminds many of another left-handed hitting Japanese slugger who came to the United States. Chicago White Sox 1B Munetaka Murakami, who, in his first MLB season, launched 35 home runs with a 16.6% walk rate, albeit with a .207 batting average and 35.4% strikeout rate. Sato is viewed as a better athlete, but expected to offer a similar offensive profile in the "three true outcomes" department, with power, walks and strikeouts.

This profile has value in fantasy, but Murakami averaged only 2.1 ESPN fantasy points per game, outside the top 100 hitters. He was the No. 127 hitter on the Player Rater, even though only nine hitters slugged more home runs. Should potential Sato investors expect better numbers than Murakami's debut? Sato may boast better plate discipline and a better likelihood to adjust his approach, perhaps trading some power for better contact. Fangraphs projects a .247 batting average and 30 home runs. While Murakami is not among ESPN's initial top 200 for points formats, Sato should earn a better ranking, though not among the top 100.

Though Sato is likely ticketed for an outfield corner with the Cubs, he will be eligible at third base only in fantasy drafts based on his games played in Japan in 2026. He can earn additional eligibility with 10 games played at another position in 2027. -- Karabell (11/24)

Royce Lewis traded to Dodgers
Lewis, 27 and a former first-round pick of the Twins in 2017, has long been ticketed for slugging stardom, but his road to becoming one of the premier, power-hitting third basemen has been bumpy. Lewis hit 15 home runs and knocked in 52 over 58 games and 239 PA during his breakout 2023 campaign, with a .920 OPS. Injuries have derailed him since, as Lewis has neither reached 20 home runs in a season nor approached a .800 OPS.

At least Lewis managed to stay healthy enough to reach 500 PA for the first time in 2026, though he struck out in 25.5% of his PA with a career-low 71.9% contact rate. Can the Los Angeles Dodgers get him consistently productive and keep him on the field? The Minnesota Twins clearly could not. Eligible at first base and third base, perhaps the Dodgers view Lewis as a utility option and lefty killer, but if he doesn't hit, it doesn't matter. Bump Lewis up your draft sheets a bit because of this trade, but he remains more of a late-round sleeper than a sure thing. -- Karabell 11/20

Maikel Garcia traded to Mariners

Garcia, 26, suffered through a rough 2026 season, missing months with hamstring and hand injuries, and slugging only .381 during his 82 games and 344 PA. Not that Garcia is a renowned power hitter, but he delivered 16 home runs among his 60 extra-base hits in a breakout 2025, along with 23 stolen bases, after stealing 37 bases in 2024. Garcia missed only seven games during 2024-25, so volume played a role when he finished 18th among hitters in 2025 fantasy points.

A 2025 Gold Glove winner, Garcia is one of the better defensive third basemen in baseball, and he should solidify the position for Seattle. However, while we don't know for sure where he will hit in his new lineup -- and leaving one hitter-challenging home ballpark in Kansas City for another does not help him -- it figures to be near the bottom half, which caps his fantasy upside. Expect Garcia to bounce back to some degree offensively, with his early ESPN 2027 points ranking featuring him positively as the No. 10 3B and just outside the top 100. -- Karabell (11/18)

Other free agents: Eugenio Suarez, Edmundo Sosa, Yoan Moncada, Si Hwan Roh (posted)

Outfield

Some free agents: George Springer, Trent Grisham, Ian Happ, Seiya Suzuki (Q), Randy Arozarena, Taylor Ward, Daulton Varsho, Adolis Garcia, Luis Robert Jr., Randal Grichuk, Myles Straw, Lane Thomas

Designated hitter

Some free agents: Joc Pederson, Dominic Smith

Starting pitcher
Kevin Gausman signs with Tigers
Gausman, 35, made 32 starts for the Blue Jays and Cubs in 2026, though his 4.51 ERA and 1.27 WHIP were his worst marks since the 2019 season, and he failed to win double digit games. Blame a spike in home runs and a bit of bad luck, as his BABIP was up 48 points from the prior season. Gausman remains durable and he is still missing plenty of bats (184 strikeouts). The Tigers need those attributes in filling their rotation, and while fantasy managers may not like the ERA, Gausman was a top 50 starting pitcher in fantasy points thanks to the volume. He should be among the top 50 starters in 2027 drafts as well, with upside for the top 30, just like his prior seasons with Toronto. -- Karabell (11/25)

Toronto Blue Jays sign SP Kaima Taira
Having missed out on their top free-agent pitching prize, Tarik Skubal, the Blue Jays moved quickly to sign Taira, who by many accounts had the second-best raw stuff of any pitcher on this winter's market, to a five-year, $80 million contract. Taira spent seven of his first eight seasons in Japan as a reliever but transitioned beautifully to a starting pitching role in 2026, posting a Nippon Professional Baseball-leading 1.36 ERA across 22 starts and one relief appearance. Prior to that, he had posted sub-2 ERAs in each of his prior five seasons working out of the bullpen (2020-22, '24-25), 31 saves in 2025, as well as a 2.40 ERA in 23 starts while pitching out of the rotation in 2023.

That's a remarkable level of success for a pitcher who stands just 5-foot-8. Marcus Stroman is the only MLB pitcher this century who stood that height or shorter to have made as many as 10 starts. Taira's extension -- measuring the distance from the pitching rubber that the pitcher releases the baseball -- is regarded as elite, however, and to a point where he'd likely rank in the upper quarter in U.S. play in that department. Between that and his six -- and, by some accounts, as many as eight -- pitches in his repertoire, he counters the height question with a great deal of upside. Taira's command of his pitch mix is considered elite, and generally ground ball-generating, so even with some anticipated regression to his strikeout rate he might well deliver numbers that place among the top 40 pitchers in fantasy baseball.

We'll see how swiftly and smoothly Taira adapts to U.S. play, which despite becoming less demanding upon starting pitchers in the post-COVID era, still has a lengthier and more physically taxing schedule. Questions about whether he's more suited for relief than rotation work are valid, and the primary obstacle towards him earning that potential top-40 starter ranking. By signing in Toronto, where he's more likely to have the team's patience with his adapting to the rotation, Saito will earn a ranking around No. 75 at the position, in the Joey Cantillo/Trey Yesavage/Eduardo Rodriguez range. -- Cockcroft (11/24)

Freddy Peralta signs with Orioles
Peralta, 30, ended the 2026 season with a bloated 4.42 ERA and 1.33 WHIP, but those numbers hardly tell the story. The longtime Brewers ace who struck out 200 hitters during three consecutive seasons started the 2026 season with the Mets after an offseason trade, and things went poorly right away. Then, months later, the Mets traded Peralta to the Rays and, voila, all was well again!

With his mechanics tweaked and his approach refined (more changeups, fewer sliders), Peralta posted a 3.25 ERA and 1.01 WHIP during 10 Rays starts, albeit with a lower strikeout rate than typical, but at least he was good. Then he thrived in the postseason, winning ALCS MVP honors. That is what fantasy managers expect. Peralta may not be a top 20 starting pitcher for fantasy, but he should be close. Peralta ranks among the top 100 players for points and roto formats. -- Karabell (11/24)

Trevor Rogers signs with Cubs
Rogers, 29, was never going to match his incredible 2025 season, when he posted a 1.81 ERA and 0.90 WHIP during 18 starts, but his 2026 campaign (4.03, 1.18) may have still exceeded some expectations. After all, the 6-foot-5 left-hander posted a 4.92 ERA and 1.58 WHIP for the Marlins and Orioles in 2024. The 2017 first-round pick dealt with injuries, control issues and inconsistency for much of his career, among other things. Then, suddenly, he was a star, even for half a season.

Rogers probably isn't a star. The Cubs get a guy who made 30 starts (for the first time) and did his best work in the second half, with a 3.52 ERA and 1.04 WHIP, whiffing 27% of hitters. That's good, reliable work, and Rogers was among the top 40 starting pitchers in ESPN fantasy points. Can the Cubs and fantasy managers get that version in 2027? That seems reasonable. Rogers isn't an ace, but worthy of being among the top 40 starters in drafts. There is nothing wrong with that. -- Karabell (11/24)

Tarik Skubal signs with Mets

Two winters ago, the New York Mets opened their wallet to get their offensive centerpiece, Juan Soto. On Sunday, the Mets did the same to get a centerpiece for their rotation, and for a similarly record-setting deal, signing Tarik Skubal to a nine-year, $450 million contract.

Fortunately for us in fantasy, we won't need to spend as much as the Mets did to add Skubal to our rosters, but it's a good landing spot for the lefty. He'll call one of the more pitching-leaning ballparks in Citi Field his home through 2036. -- Cockcroft (11/23)

For a more in-depth look at the fantasy impact of Skubal's signing, click here.

Luis Castillo and Davis Martin traded to Rockies
What happens when the league's worst non-Rockies or Athletics pitcher (minimum 130 innings) comes to Coors Field? We're about to find out. Castillo entered 2026 riding a four-year streak with at least 350 fantasy points, 160 strikeouts and a sub-1.20 WHIP. However, a progressive drop in his velocity and a rise in his fly ball rate during that time caused him to unravel last year, first for the Seattle Mariners and then catastrophically so following his midseason trade to the Chicago White Sox. Castillo's year ended with a shoulder injury, so in addition to the Coors factor, he enters 2027 facing many questions.

Martin, meanwhile, was the far superior fantasy pitcher between these two -- by almost two times in terms of point production (242-127). Martin, though, ended 2026 on a similarly sour note. He had a 9-2 record and 2.41 ERA through his first 13 starts, but went 0-8 with a 5.72 ERA thereafter. He dealt with a calf issue, a blister and concerns that he might be tipping pitches, ultimately making only a mop-up appearance during Chicago's playoff run.

Martin was nevertheless the piece the Rockies wanted in order to agree to absorb Castillo's remaining contract. Both will probably eat innings for a Rockies rotation always in need of depth. Either could be a "matchup candidate" in road games, if they seem to have righted the ship during spring training -- which is why a lockout-influenced, shortened preseason would be detrimental to both. Still, neither pitcher is a draft-day option, given their new team. -- Cockcroft (11/20)

Twins sign Sonny Gray
Gray, now 37 years old, returns to Minnesota after a three-year detour through St. Louis and Boston. He has enjoyed a bit of a career rebirth later in his career, averaging 385.8 fantasy points over the past four seasons, and never deviating by more than 25 points in either direction in any individual year. Gray's consistency is a valuable thing in fantasy leagues, particularly points-based scoring, where his good ratios and solid innings totals are most advantageous.

That said, a two-year pattern of declining average fastball velocity and strikeout rates raises concerns that regression might hit him harder than a typical frontline starter, if not in 2027 then perhaps if he doesn't opt out and continues into his 39-year-old campaign in 2028. I've got Gray ranked amongst my top 25 fantasy starting pitchers, and within the top 75 overall, and I'd expect he will (and should) generally be drafted in that range.

Gray's acquisition, however, gives the Twins at least nine viable rotation candidates, creating a logjam of popular deep-mixed/AL-only names like Mick Abel, Zebby Matthews, Connor Prielipp for fourth/fifth starter spots. Perhaps a trade is forthcoming, preferably for some hitting to bolster the lineup and give Gray more run support, but otherwise this is a spring battle that'll be high on the list of those to watch. Only Gray, Joe Ryan, Taj Bradley and Pablo Lopez would figure to be locks. -- Cockcroft (11/18)

Bryce Miller traded to Royals
Miller, 28, emerged as a standout fantasy option for the Seattle Mariners in 2024, winning 12 games and posting a 2.94 ERA and 0.98 WHIP. Injuries and inconsistency have plagued the right-hander since then, as Miller won only eight of 39 starts in 2025-26 with a 4.82 ERA and 1.26 WHIP while permitting 38 home runs. Elbow woes ruined his 2025 campaign, and he missed the first six weeks of 2026 with an oblique injury.

Still, when Miller is healthy, he can be effective. He posted a 2.18 ERA and 0.83 WHIP prior to the 2026 All-Star break before a rough second half (and myriad home runs) ruined things. Moving from one pitcher's park in Seattle to another in Kansas City shouldn't be a factor, but at least Miller should be guaranteed a rotation spot, which was in question in Seattle. Miller is certainly a sleeper candidate to regain his place among the top 30 starting pitchers in fantasy, but ESPN's preliminary points ranking features Miller well outside the top 50 starting pitchers. -- Karabell (11/18)

Dustin May signs with White Sox

May, 29, made 31 mostly league-average starts for the Cardinals and eventual champion Brewers this season -- many of them quite abbreviated. In fact, he ended up averaging fewer than four innings over his 10 Brewers starts and he did not qualify for the ERA title. The desperate White Sox figure to allow May to go deeper into games, but that comes at a cost, since he posted a 4.70 ERA and a 1.32 WHIP with only 0.4 bWAR last season.

Hey, at least May stayed healthy, which is a feat for him. Plus, he was a bit unlucky, as his 3.54 FIP indicates. However, that doesn't mean May warrants inclusion in ESPN standard drafts, with a preliminary points-league rank outside the top 75 starting pitchers. -- Karabell (11/18)

Other free agents: Michael King, Robbie Ray, Brandon Woodruff, Zac Gallen, Shota Imanaga, Chris Bassitt, Jack Flaherty, Jameson Taillon, Max Scherzer, Clay Holmes, Matthew Boyd, Nick Pivetta, Shane Bieber, Nick Martinez, Tyler Mahle, Foster Griffin, Michael Soroka

Relief pitcher
Emilio Pagan signs with Tigers
Pagan, 35, saved 57 games for the Cincinnati Reds over the past two seasons, although his 2025 numbers were rather ordinary (3.38 ERA, 25.9% K rate). Still, this is a franchise that desired Kenley Jansen and let him save 22 games last season even though there were better pitchers in the bullpen. Pagan produced nearly identical stats to Jansen. In other words, Pagan isn't so valuable -- but if all you care about are saves in a roto format, a healthy Pagan should provide at least 25 of them. -- Karabell (11/13)

Evan Phillips signs with Braves
Phillips, 32, posted a 2.36 ERA over parts of six seasons for the Los Angeles Dodgers. He also accrued 42 combined saves during 2023 and 2024. He missed most of 2025 dealing with Tommy John surgery and returned last season to pitch 26 effective innings. Additionally, Phillips has never permitted a run over 18⅓ postseason innings. The Braves figure to turn to Robert Suarez to close (because Raisel Iglesias is a free agent), but a healthy Phillips should accrue ample holds as well as occasional saves. -- Karabell (11/13)

Other free agents: Raisel Iglesias, Pete Fairbanks, Carlos Estevez, A.J. Minter, Blake Treinen, Martin Perez, Gregory Soto, Kenley Jansen, Hiromi Itoh (posted)

stories.headline: Luis Enrique praises Roma after draw halts PSG's winning streak
stories.summary: Paris Saint-Germain coach Luis Enrique said Roma was his team's "toughest match of this season" after a hard-fought 2-2 Champions League draw on Wednesday.
stories.body:
Paris Saint-Germain coach Luis Enrique praised AS Roma for handing the defending Champions League title holder their toughest test of the season after the Italian side snapped PSG's 12-game winning streak with a 2-2 draw on Wednesday.

"Without any doubt this was our toughest match of this season, in the Champions League or the French league. I am happy with the result, and the merit goes to Roma," Luis Enrique said.

"Facing a team with this attitude and this kind of mentality is very hard to play against. It's very different to the kind of match we're used to."

Roma striker Donyell Malen secured the point in the 78th minute, blasting in a penalty to end a dominant run in which PSG had not dropped points since losing at home to Monaco on Sept. 4.

Luis Enrique also lauded Roma counterpart Gian Piero Gasperini's tactical setup and said he hopes to face him again in the knockout rounds.

"It's the first time I've come up against him as a coach," he said before pausing and nodding in respect.

"It's better to talk about Roma's future, not PSG's. Roma's future is wonderful; they can win the Scudetto. I have no doubt they can finish in the top 24, I hope so, and I wouldn't like to face them again. Maybe in the final," the Spanish coach added.

Malen, who entered midway through the second half after scoring four goals in a 5-1 win at Parma on Saturday, found the net again with his 17th goal in 16 games this season, including five in the Champions League.

"At the moment he is among the very best strikers in the world, with his ability to score goals, his pace, the speed with which he shoots as well," Gasperini said. "He took a bit of time to get going when he came on, but by the end we saw the real Malen. He took the penalty very well."

Gasperini explained that he held Malen back until the second half because of his heavy workload for Roma and the Netherlands.

"I go back to Rome very, very happy tonight," Gasperini said. "It was a great performance against a team which is no doubt the best in the world at the moment. It was an important test and a very difficult one for us."

Before kickoff, PSG's ultras boldly displayed a giant tifo depicting two bloodied Roman gladiators -- the victorious figure dressed in PSG's blue, white, and red, and the defeated gladiator kneeling with bowed head in Roma's red and gold.

Information from The Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Maple Leafs support Sergei Bobrovsky during rough start in Toronto
stories.summary: Sergei Bobrovsky is off to the worst start of a career that will almost certainly land him in the Hockey Hall of Fame.
stories.body:
NEWARK, N.J. -- Sergei Bobrovsky is off to the worst start of a career that will almost certainly land him in the Hockey Hall of Fame.

Toronto Maple Leafs teammate Kirill Marchenko does not worry about his fellow Russian's struggles in their day-to-day interactions.

"I just say, 'Good morning, Sergei,' and he says, 'Good morning, Marchy,'" he said. "I said, 'How are you doing?' He said: 'I'm good. How about you?' 'I'm good too.' And like, 'Let's go and do breakfast together.'''

Breakfast has not been the problem for the goaltender affectionately known as "Bob." His performance has been.

Bobrovsky has lost 11 of the 14 games he has played in with an .874 save percentage that ranks third worst in the NHL among those with at least 10 starts. His 3.65 goals-against average is the sixth highest in the league.

"I've got full faith in Bob," coach Jim Hiller said after an energetic practice Wednesday following a day off in New York and a victory at the Islanders Monday night that ended his team's losing streak at nine games.

"It's Bob. He's an outstanding goaltender. There's been a lot made of it, but that's not coming from us internally at all, so we're ready for him to get in there and play. That's the bottom line."

The Maple Leafs recalled Artur Akhtyamov from the minors, but Hiller said Bobrovsky is set to start Saturday at Pittsburgh after Anthony Stolarz plays Friday at Boston. The Bruins game will be Stolarz's sixth time in net in their past seven.

"Stolie's played well, so we ride Stolie here just a little bit," Hiller said. "The schedule's worked out for that."

Committing to Bobrovsky is not working out great for Toronto, which signed him to a three-year contract worth $21 million. The two-time Vezina Trophy winner and Stanley Cup champion turned 38 in September and also had a sub-.870 save percentage last season with Florida.

The Panthers opted not to bring Bobrovsky back, bidding farewell to one of their most important players on back-to-back title runs. Leafs players insist they are not concerned about him.

"Everybody respect him so much, and everybody knows he knows what he needs to do, and he [has] big experience," Marchenko said. "He will figure out. We just support him, but he is totally fine. He does his workouts, like all stuff, and ready to go."

Bobrovsky was requested by reporters and not made available Wednesday. Other players were instead asked how they help him through this.

"Just like you would anybody," forward Colton Sissons said. 'We don't really have anybody on different pedestals that you can't approach, and no matter how long you played in this league, when you struggle, sometimes you just need a friend to talk with. And Bob does his thing and he's such a true pro."

Marchenko is expected to play in Boston after missing the past 12 games with what is believed to be a left knee injury.

"I feel healthy," he said. "I'm healthy and ready to go."

Marchenko had 14 points in 14 games before getting hurt. He skated with Nick Paul and captain Auston Matthews at practice.

"A huge addition," said Gavin McKenna, the No. 1 pick who scored the winning goal Monday night. "We felt it when he wasn't in the lineup. He's one of those guys who's super fun energy to be around, and obviously on the ice you see what he does. He's a great player. Yeah, we're looking forward to getting him back."

Sissons is also expected to be back after missing the past seven games. Toronto lost six of them.

"You just want to be a part of the solution," Sissons said. "When you're on the sidelines, it's tough -- frustrating and you want to help kind of dig your way out of it."

McKenna did not get back on the ice for a single shift after putting the Leafs ahead with 11:05 left at the Islanders.

"When you score, you obviously want to get back out there," McKenna said. "But in a game like that, where I thought I played pretty well -- at the end of the day, I was OK with that. I was happy with my game and the team getting the win. I think you want to be out there, but at the end of the day, it's OK."

Hiller has benched McKenna several times through the first 26 games of the season.

"I want him to take away the fact that we won the game and that he was a really important part of it," Toronto's first-year coach said. "We talked on the bench during the game. He was ready to roll. We could've used him again if things changed a little bit. But it just turned out that he didn't get back out there."

McKenna said Hiller told him he'd play if there was another offensive zone faceoff. There was not.

"I think he knows that I want to be in those chances and stuff like that," McKenna said. "We've had conversations about it. That day'll come at some point. Just got to keep building that trust with him and keep doing the little things right and then I think when that day comes, hopefully I can do whatever I can do to make sure that I stay in those situations."

stories.headline: 2026 NBA Cup: Schedule, format, groups, updates and more
stories.summary: Here's everything you need to know about the fourth annual in-season tournament, including the recent wins by the Celtics and Mavericks.
stories.body:
Which two teams will face off inside Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis for the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup?

This summer, the league unveiled the full group stage schedule for this year's in-season tournament, with action taking place every Friday from Oct. 30 to Nov. 27 and on special Cup nights during Thanksgiving week (Nov. 24-25).

After the New York Knicks became the first team to win the NBA Cup and Finals in the same season, can Jalen Brunson & Co. keep their championship run going? They'll have plenty of competition, specifically within the star-studded East Group B.

Here's what you need to know about the in-season tournament, now in its fourth year.

Jump to a section:

Schedule | Groups | FAQ

Takeaways

76ers 111, Heat 104
The Miami Heat's seven-game winning streak is over, but their NBA Cup hopes are still very much alive.
Tyrese Maxey and LeBron James led the Philadelphia 76ers to a home victory over the Heat on Wednesday to deal Miami its first loss in Cup play.

Maxey led Philadelphia with a team-high 30 points, and James posted 25 points, 10 rebounds and 12 assists to register his first triple-double since signing with the 76ers during the offseason.

Philadelphia's victory left the 76ers, Heat and Cleveland Cavaliers with identical 2-1 records in East Group B. After managing to cut a 16-point Philadelphia lead to a seven-point loss, Miami retained the group's top seed with a plus-25 point differential.

Cleveland entered its final Cup game Wednesday in second place with a plus-21 point differential. Despite their victory, the 76ers are in third place in the group with a minus-12 point differential because of a previous blowout loss to the Cavaliers.

The group's winner will automatically advance to the Cup's eight-team knockout round. The group's second-place finisher will vie for a wild-card spot in the tournament. The group standings will get another shakeup pending the result of Wednesday's game between the Cavaliers and New York Knicks.

The pre-Thanksgiving showdown between Philadelphia and Miami pitted James against Giannis Antetokounmpo in a matchup of NBA Cup MVPs. James led the Los Angeles Lakers to the inaugural Cup championship in 2023, and Antetokounmpo led the Milwaukee Bucks to the 2024 Cup crown.

The 76ers improved to an East-leading 15-4 record by beating the Heat despite losing forward Jaylen Brown to hamstring tightness before halftime. Brown departed with six points in 17 minutes.

Miami will conclude its opening round Cup play Friday against New York. Also that day, Philadelphia will face the Indiana Pacers, who are 1-2 in Cup play. -- Ben Golliver

NBA Cup FAQ: Everything to know
What is the format?

NBA commissioner Adam Silver has had a longstanding fascination with European soccer. Establishing an in-season cup competition within the NBA schedule came from soccer leagues having both a regular-season title, won by the team with the most points over the full year, and a separate tournament (or, in some leagues, multiple tournaments) that runs concurrently with the league season.

In England, for example, there are the various divisions -- led by the Premier League -- and also the FA Cup competition. But unlike those European leagues, which play their cup competitions outside of their league schedules, the NBA Cup is built in to the regular-season slate.

The 30 NBA teams are split into six five-team groups -- three featuring Eastern Conference teams and three comprising Western Conference teams -- with each team then playing one game against the other four in its group. The winner of each group, plus the team with the best record among the non-group winners, advances to the knockout stage of the competition.

How will this impact the regular-season schedule and standings?

Typically, the NBA sends out a full 82-game schedule in mid-August. Now, the league sends out only 80 games and leaves a gap of roughly a week to fill in later, depending on how the group stage of the NBA Cup plays out.

The two teams from the East and West that lose in the quarterfinals will play their 82nd game against each other. Meanwhile, the 22 teams that fail to qualify for the knockout rounds will have their final two games scheduled -- one at home and one on the road against others eliminated in the group stage.

The teams that reach the NBA Cup final will actually play 83 games -- though the championship game won't count toward the standings or any statistical markers. The four teams that reach the semifinals will have completed their 82 games and won't need any other games added to their schedule.

Any team that makes it to the semifinals will have that game moved later in the schedule to avoid back-to-back games. The NBA made this change in an effort to avoid having empty days on the calendar while attempting to minimize back-to-backs for all teams as much as possible.

Where are the semifinals and final being played?

In a shift from previous tournaments, the quarterfinals and semifinals will be played at home sites. The Dec. 11 title game, meanwhile, will move from Las Vegas to the storied Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis. NBA commissioner Adam Silver previously said the league was searching for "storied college arenas" to play host to the Cup final. (No venue has been announced for 2027.)

Why does the NBA Cup include regular-season games?

Before its launch, one of the main questions surrounding the in-season tournament was why any team would be incentivized to compete in it. The NBA ensured teams will be motivated by making every game part of the season and, as in-conference matchups, potentially important to playoff tiebreakers. If this had been set up like the cup tournaments in European soccer, there would have been nothing stopping NBA teams from opting out by sitting their top players for extra rest.

Which teams make up the groups?

To create the groups, the NBA put the 15 teams in each conference into five pots, separated by their finish last season. Pot 1 included the teams that finished in the top three in the regular-season standings, Nos. 4-6 in the standings went into Pot 2, Nos. 7-9 into Pot 3, Nos. 10-12 into Pot 4 and Nos. 13-15 into Pot 5. As a result, the following groups were drawn:
